title: The noise cost of reservoir locality in broadband quantum amplifier chains
abstract: Directional quantum amplifiers enable weak-signal readout while protecting the source, but reservoir noise limits sensitivity. Finite-band suppression must reconcile frequency-dependent responses with fixed local couplings and finite rates. We construct adjacent-site loss channels attaining the known single-frequency minimum under local compatibility conditions, as an uncapped benchmark. For specified uniform and dimerized chains, we compare fixed reservoirs at matched drift, ports, high-gain band and complete gain/loss rate caps. At the representative cap $R=8$ and halfwidth $Ω=0.05$, nearest-neighbor arithmetic band average noise exceeds the unrestricted optimum by more than $1.01265$ quanta in the uniform chain for every finite $N\ge64$. Boundary-response bounds give necessary rates and targets requiring range two. At $N=64$, finite-auxiliary calculations retain a noise advantage under matched total coupling budgets; response bounds quantify noise-resolution tolerances. These theoretical results guide reservoir design and noise calibration for a proposed cryogenic microwave array with a $100$ kHz design band.

title: ReDiS: Reasoning-Diagnosis Self-Evolution for Multimodal Reasoning in Remote Sensing
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.

title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.

title: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Long-term time series forecasting requires temporal dependency modeling that remains stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy and non-stationary, making deep learning models prone to fitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. A key question is whether there exist temporal relationship structures that recur across different temporal positions and variables. We analyze temporal relationship matrices on commonly used time series datasets and find that samples from different temporal positions and different variables exhibit shared dominant temporal relationship structures. This indicates that temporal relationship structures contain patterns that recur stably across samples and variables. To learn such shared structures, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network for directly learning shared and generalizable temporal dependencies. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared structural constraints, rather than fitting incidental interactions in a fully unconstrained manner. Notably, this simple structure-aware design consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all datasets, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency.

title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
abstract: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $Θ(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.

title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF

title: Confine to the Task, Anchor the Rest: Concept-Guided Retention Regularizer for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.

title: Learning a Group Element from Its Action: Galois Correspondences, Optimal ERM, and an Abel-Ruffini Threshold for the Natarajan Dimension
abstract: We study learning an unknown element $g$ of a group acting with finite orbits on a countable set, from examples $(x,gx)$. After a sample on $A$, the consistent hypotheses are the restrictions of a coset of the pointwise stabilizer of $A$, and the sample forces exactly the labels of points this stabilizer fixes; for a Galois group, they form the field generated by the data. Through this correspondence, multiclass dimensions become group invariants: the DS and graph dimensions equal the height, the Littlestone dimension the longest irredundant sequence length, and the teaching dimension the minimal base size. Among deterministic learners, symmetry makes empirical risk minimization optimal: on nondegenerate classes every consistent learner, whatever its tie-breaking, attains the optimal realizable sample complexity up to constant factors, and every consistent online learner the optimal mistake bound. Agnostically, every ERM's sample complexity exceeds the known lower bound by at most the DS-to-Natarajan ratio, up to constants. For finite Galois extensions of countable fields, the Natarajan dimension equals a group invariant, the coset-cube number, which is at least the number of complemented factors of any chief series of any subgroup. Hence the dimensions coincide for every solvable Galois group, while for the groups $A_5$ and $S_5$ of the quintic they are $2<3$ and $3<4$, and $A_5$ is the smallest group with a gap. For the Galois group $S_n$ of the general equation of degree $n$, they coincide exactly when $n\le 4$, i.e., in characteristic zero, exactly when the equation is solvable by radicals; the implication is one-way, as the simple group $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$ has no gap. For linear, orthogonal and unitary maps of $\mathbb R^d$ or $\mathbb C^d$ both dimensions equal $d$, and a two-fibered pseudo-cube is a disjoint union of Natarajan cubes exactly when its monodromy group is abelian.

title: JANUBIY O'ZBEKISTONDA QO'RG'OSHIN–RUH MA'DANLASHUVINING G'ILON HUDUDIGA XOS FORMATSION TIPLARI: GEOLOGIK-GENETIK XUSUSIYATLARI VA PROGNOZ-QIDIRUV MEZONLARI
abstract: Maqolada Janubiy O'zbekistonning Hisor tog'lari doirasida joylashgan G'ilon istiqbolli maydonida qo'rg'oshin–ruh va kompleks polimetall ma'danlashuvini prognozlashning geologik-genetik asoslari tahlil qilindi. Rasmiy ma'lumotlarda G'ilon maydoni mis, ruh va qo'rg'oshin bo'yicha istiqbolli obyekt sifatida qayd etilgan. Janubi-g'arbiy Hisordagi Xondiza kabi yaxshi o'rganilgan kolchedan-polimetall tizimlar analog sifatida ko'rib chiqildi, biroq ularning G'ilonga to'liq tenglashtirilishi emas, balki qidiruv mezonlarini shakllantirishdagi metodik ahamiyati asoslandi. Litologik-stratigrafik, struktur-tektonik, magmatik, gidrotermal-metasomatik, mineralogik va geokimyoviy belgilarni birgalikda baholash asosida istiqbolli uchastkalarni reytinglash sxemasi taklif etildi. Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag assotsiatsiyalari, sfalerit–galenit–pirit–xalkopirit mineral majmuasi, uzilmalar kesishgan zonalar va gidrotermal o'zgarishlar asosiy qidiruv indikatorlari sifatida ajratildi.

title: A Three-Layer Architecture for Human-Interpretable Machine Reasoning.
abstract: Abstract Modern AI solvers can generate correct solutions to complex problems, yet their internal reasoning remains inaccessible to human decision‑makers. This document proposes a modular architecture designed to make advanced machine reasoning transparent and interpretable. The system consists of three coordinated layers: a Solver, which performs high‑speed reasoning; a Trace System, which reconstructs the solver’s full reasoning path into a structured map; and an Interpreter, which translates that map into human‑understandable concepts, narratives, and implications. While solver systems already exist in early form, the trace and interpreter layers remain undeveloped. This proposal outlines the missing components required to build an integrated, human‑interpretable reasoning pipeline and establishes a foundation for future research, collaboration, and development.

title: Evaluación de arquitecturas RAG descentralizadas para la reducción de alucinaciones y mejora de la trazabilidad en entornos corporativos simulados
abstract: La incorporación de modelos de lenguaje de gran escala en entornos organizacionales requiere mecanismos que permitan mejorar la recuperación de información y reducir la generación de respuestas no sustentadas en fuentes verificables. El objetivo del estudio fue evaluar una arquitectura de generación aumentada por recuperación (Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG) descentralizada orientada a mejorar la trazabilidad de la información y reducir las alucinaciones en entornos corporativos simulados. Se implementó un entorno experimental basado en un corpus sintético de 10000 documentos corporativos distribuidos en repositorios vectoriales federados. La arquitectura propuesta integró cuatro componentes principales: ingesta distribuida, almacenamiento vectorial federado, enrutamiento semántico y mecanismos de validación de respuestas mediante guardrails. Se evaluaron escenarios comparativos entre arquitecturas centralizadas y descentralizadas utilizando métricas de tiempo hasta el primer token (TTFT), tasa de alucinación, fidelidad de respuesta mediante RAGAS y validación humana. Los resultados evidenciaron una reducción del TTFT desde 3,2 s hasta 0,4 s en consultas complejas y una disminución de la tasa de alucinación desde 32,0 % hasta 1,9 % en el entorno experimental evaluado. evidence.abstract: La incorporación de modelos de lenguaje de gran escala en entornos organizacionales requiere mecanismos que permitan mejorar la recuperación de información y reducir la generación de respuestas no sustentadas en fuentes verificables. title: Gaussian approximation for linear stochastic approximation with an application to reinforcement learning
abstract: Рассматривается задача статистического вывода для решения системы линейных уравнений A ¯ θ ⋆ = b ¯ , в которой матрица A и вектор b неизвестны, а вместо них доступны зашумлённые наблюдения. Исследуется метод линейной стохастической аппроксимации с постоянным шагом и марковским шумом. Усреднение Поляка–Рупперта (PR) снижает дисперсию, но сохраняет стационарное смещение порядка α , ухудшающее нормальную аппроксимацию. Для устранения ведущего смещения используется экстраполяция Ричардсона–Ромберга: средние двух рекурсий с шагами α и 2 α , использующих одну и ту же траекторию марковской цепи, объединяются в одну оценку. Показано, что такая коррекция улучшает нормальную аппроксимацию без изменения предельной дисперсии. Получена неасимптотическая оценка в расстоянии Колмогорова для скалярных проекций PR-усреднений с экстраполяцией Ричардсона–Ромберга. Для траектории длины n при выборе шага порядка n − 1 / 2 полученная верхняя граница убывает как n − 1 / 4 с точностью до логарифмических множителей. В качестве приложения исследуемой теории рассматривается построение доверительных интервалов для параметров, оцениваемых алгоритмом TD(0) в обучении с подкреплением. Численные эксперименты на синтетических данных подтверждают коррекцию среднего и улучшение покрытия доверительных интервалов без заметного увеличения их ширины.

title: AIRIME: a scalable adaptive RIME algorithm for feature optimization and data-driven monkeypox disease prediction
abstract: The rapid growth of big data in recent applications has created a pressing need for scalable and efficient optimization algorithms capable of handling large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Addressing this challenge, an Adaptive Improved Rime-Ice Optimization algorithm (AIRIME) is proposed which is built on the physics-based RIME algorithm inspired by the formation of soft and hard rime on surfaces. While RIME offers a strong theoretical foundation, it is hindered by limited exploratory capability, slow convergence, and an imbalance between exploration and exploitation. AIRIME introduces four key enhancements, including Adaptive k-Average-Best Mutation (AKAB), Adaptive Searching Process (ASP), Enhanced Solution Quality (ESQ), and Gaussian-Based Optimal Solution Mutation (GBOM), to overcome these challenges and meet the requirements of big data applications. AIRIME was rigorously tested on 41 functions from the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites, outperforming various classical, recent and advanced algorithms. Statistical evaluations, including Friedman rank and Wilcoxon rank tests, validated its superior performance and robustness. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrated the adaptability and efficiency of the proposed strategies. Moreover, a binary version of AIRIME was applied to feature selection (FS) tasks across 14 datasets, achieving promising results compared to various established binary metaheuristics. Furthermore, its real-world applicability was demonstrated in a novel Monkeypox disease prediction framework, where AIRIME helped to achieve an exceptional classification accuracy of 95.52% while selecting significantly fewer features, underscoring its efficiency in classifying high-dimensional healthcare data. Thus, AIRIME represents a significant advancement in big data-driven optimization, combining scalability, adaptability, and robustness to address complex and high-dimensional challenges across various domains, including critical healthcare applications.

title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.

title: RepProbe: Can Video Language Models Count Repeated Actions? A Diagnostic Benchmark
abstract: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/

title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics
abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from π_{0.5} and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and downstream diagnostic updating through not only diagnostic accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, and elicited probability and information entropy. Starting experiments from the breakdown at the level of capabilities, to the diagnosis of the pre-event state before the evidence arrives, and to the post-event state transition after the evidence arrives, our research has revealed the profound limitations and internal causes existing in the dynamic diagnostic process. At the same time, we have also conducted sufficient verification and generalization experiments to prove that these limitations are widespread. Together, these findings shift the central challenge from whether LLMs possess relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and effectively use the right evidence under clinical diagnosis and conduct a more detailed mechanism analysis to identify the exact location of the capability gap.

title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching
abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid misalignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose conebeam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain selfsupervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

title: Beyond ICD Codes: Semantic IDs for Generative Medical Coding
abstract: Generative approaches to automatic International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding use large language models (LLMs) to predict ICD codes from clinical documents. However, original ICD code strings are not ideal generation targets because the ICD hierarchy does not always reflect clinical relationships, and LLMs struggle to interpret and generate these codes. We introduce SemICD, a framework that trains LLMs to generate Semantic IDs (SIDs) instead. SemICD constructs SIDs by hierarchically clustering embeddings of textual code profiles, allowing semantically related codes to share prefixes while each complete SID uniquely identifies one ICD code. To align the SID tokens with clinical semantics, we employ two auxiliary tasks for bidirectional generation between textual code profiles and SIDs. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLMs show that SemICD outperforms direct code generation, improving Micro-F1 by 1.34-8.00 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/youwillbethebest/SemICD.

title: MIND: Instruction-Conditioned Incremental Grounding for Robots
abstract: Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target-room decisions without re-evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 evaluations against 15 to 18. Additional materials are available at https://mind-icra27.github.io/.

On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.

title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

title: Mapping AI Adoption in Digital Marketing: A Bibliometric Analysis, Systematic Literature Review, and Future Research Agenda
abstract: This study aims to map the development of artificial intelligence adoption in digital marketing, identify dominant themes, examine methodological approaches, theoretical foundations, and empirical contexts, and formulate research gaps and a future research agenda. The study employs a combined design integrating bibliometric analysis and a systematic literature review. Data were obtained from 94 articles published during 2018–2026 and selected through the stages of identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. Bibliometric analysis was used to examine publication trends, journals, countries, citations, collaboration, and relationships among keywords, while VOSviewer was used to generate network visualization, density visualization, and overlay visualization. The results show that publications have grown rapidly, with a temporary peak in 2025. Dominant themes include artificial intelligence, digital marketing, machine learning, social media, generative AI, customer experience, trust, transparency, privacy, and personalization. Previous studies have been dominated by quantitative approaches, cross-sectional designs, and SEM analysis, with Signaling Theory being one of the most frequently used theoretical foundations. The main gaps include inconsistent definitions of AI adoption, limited longitudinal designs, weak integration of technical, organizational, and behavioral aspects, and limited attention to responsible AI and negative consequences. This study concludes that AI adoption in digital marketing should be understood as a gradual, multidimensional socio-technical process requiring the integration of technological capabilities, organizational readiness, consumer responses, and ethical governance.

title: Le Chapeau: An A/B Testing Platform for Socratic AI in Education
abstract: Le Chapeau is a turnkey experimental platform designed for educational and behavioral researchers to deploy controlled web chat applications comparing AI interaction paradigms (such as baseline control, direct instructional assistant, and Socratic questioning tutor) with real-time data persistence and salted deterministic anonymization.

title: raefalizadehnima-droid/Sustainable-Pathways-to-Trustworthy-AI-in-Pharmaceutical-Manufacturing: XAII
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is growing in pharmaceutical manufacturing, but regulatory assimilation has been slow due to difficulties in interpretability, uncertainty calibration and sustainability assessment. This work proposes a quantitative framework for assessing trustworthy AI through a multi-objective Composite Trust Index (CTI). The framework combines model predictive performance (R², RMSE), uncertainty measures (predictive variance and Expected Calibration Error), interpretability stability and sustainability metrics such as Process Mass Intensity (PMI), and is formulated for four AI paradigms: explainable AI (XAI), human-in-the-loop (HITL), hybrid physics-informed AI and uncertainty quantification (UQ).

title: 6G-HW10: 6G-Oriented Heterogeneous Waveform Dataset
abstract: 6G-HW10: 6G-Oriented Heterogeneous Waveform Dataset 6G-HW10 is a controlled synthetic dataset for heterogeneous waveform and modulation recognition from short complex-baseband observations. It combines traditional single-carrier modulation schemes, OFDM-based waveforms, OTFS-like and AFDM-like constructions, and a two-user downlink NOMA superposition under shared channel and RF-impairment parameter distributions. Key Features • Ten classes: BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK, QAM16, QAM64, CP-OFDM, DFT-s-OFDM, OTFS-like, AFDM-like and DL-NOMA-QPSK.• SNR range: −20 to +18 dB in 2 dB increments, with 1,000 observations per class/SNR combination.• Dataset size: 200,000 observations, each containing 256 complex samples represented as float32 I/Q with shape (2, 256).• Controlled simulation: shared settings for filtering, transmitter nonlinearity, time-varying multipath, carrier-frequency offset, phase noise, I/Q imbalance, amplitude variation, receive-window uncertainty and complex AWGN.• Fixed benchmark split: 160,000 training, 20,000 validation and 20,000 test observations, corresponding to 800/100/100 observations per class/SNR combination. Split seed: 2026. Data Format The dataset is supplied directly as a single HDF5 file, 6G-HW10.h5: X: I/Q observations, shape (200000, 2, 256), float32.Y: Integer class labels, shape (200000,), int16, values 0–9; these are not one-hot labels.Z: Nominal SNR in dB, shape (200000,), int16.class_names: The fixed class-label mapping.snr_values_db: The 20 nominal SNR levels.splits: Original zero-based training, validation and test indices.sample_metadata: 29 aligned generation-diagnostic arrays.metadata: Generation settings, field descriptions and source checksums. All signal values, labels, fixed split indices and per-sample metadata are preserved through lossless conversion from the frozen source dataset. README.txt explains the data structure, generation settings, scope and Python loading procedure. No ZIP extraction is required. Design Goals and Applications The dataset supports comparisons of heterogeneous signal classifiers, studies of representations for short I/Q observations, and evaluation across controlled SNR conditions. The fixed samples and split allow comparisons under the same benchmark conditions. Diagnostic metadata are not default inputs to the I/Q-only classification task. Research Context “6G-oriented” identifies the research motivation and selected waveform families. OTFS and AFDM have been investigated as candidate waveforms for next-generation wireless systems [1,2]. Here, OTFS-like and AFDM-like denote the implemented research constructions. The data are controlled synthetic observations, not standardized 6G air-interface transmissions or over-the-air measurements. No particular physical sampling rate, carrier frequency or mobility scenario is established. The two-file edition provides data and the fixed split, without the original generator or model-training code. References [1] M. Nie et al., “Towards Standardizing OTFS: A Candidate Waveform for Next-Generation Wireless Networks,” arXiv:2601.15048, 2026 (preprint). https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15048 [2] H. S. Rou et al., “Affine Frequency Division Multiplexing (AFDM) for 6G: Properties, Features, and Challenges,” IEEE Communications Standards Magazine, DOI: 10.1109/MCOMSTD.2025.3643183. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21704 Licence The dataset and README are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0). title: AI MATHEMATICAL DISCOVERY & INTERGENERATIONAL KNOWLEDGE EVOLUTION AT THE LIMIT A High-Density Research-Design Monograph on AI Reasoning, Formal Verification, and Mathematical Knowledge Succession STARLI | White Rainbow Civilization Mathematical Frontier Trilogy — Volume III Research-design edition | 13 October 2026 DESCRIPTION How can mathematical research remain inspectable, reproducible, corrigible, and useful to future generations when artificial intelligence participates in conjecture formation and proof discovery? This independently authored research-design monograph investigates this question through a three-component framework: AI Mathematical Reasoning × Formal Verification × Intergenerational Knowledge Evolution. Volume III completes a planned trilogy by shifting the focus from mathematical proof structures (Volume I) and cross-domain structural synthesis (Volume II) toward the institutions, formal artifacts, epistemic boundaries, and preservation methods needed for responsible AI-assisted mathematics. It proposes research protocols rather than claiming to establish new mathematical theorems. The monograph comprises 82 thematic chapters, each with one chapter-opening research relation and 12 individually paginated research units. Its six parts address: (I) research-oriented AI mathematical reasoning; (II) Lean, proof objects, and formal verification; (III) mathematician–AI collaboration and independent review; (IV) conjecture generation and counterexample search; (V) mathematical knowledge graphs, provenance, and proof archaeology; and (VI) long-term mathematical succession, model retirement, and open research governance. The final sections present 200 numbered Research Gates (G401–G600 in the trilogy-wide sequence) and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Research Gates are designed as executable entrances into unresolved work: each specifies an open question, a proposed test, an adversarial or stopping condition, and the evidence required for independent reassessment. The Answer Embryos are provisional research instruments that can be falsified, repaired, branched, or retired. A separate workbook indexes the chapters, research units, gates, candidate answers, and equation cards. The opening scientific preface contains 30 high-level physics derivation-route cards accompanied by conceptual three-dimensional geometric studies. Each of the 200 Research Gates and 33 Answer Embryos includes one distinct physics equation card, for a total of 233 equations. These retain their meaning within their original physical regimes; they are not presented as proofs of the book's claims about AI systems or mathematics. PRIMARY-SOURCE CONTEXT AND SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARIES The publicly available OpenAI Mathematics repository lists 719 manuscripts grouped into 372 families as of the public README consulted on 13 October 2026. These figures describe the reference catalogue and do not imply that this monograph has read or independently validated all underlying proofs. Repository content has varied in public versions; manuscript-specific claims should always be checked against their primary texts, available formalizations, citations, and version histories. Formal verification of an encoded theorem is not equivalent to proving that the encoded statement perfectly captures the original informal claim. Likewise, mathematical plausibility, numerical experiments, AI consensus, and persuasive exposition are not substitutes for deductive proof. The work is independent of OpenAI. It does not assert ownership of the original repository manuscripts, certify their correctness, or claim empirical results for the proposed research protocols. Its central contribution is an explicit research architecture in which negative findings, source corrections, independent reproduction, rights boundaries, and the freedom of successor investigators to challenge or replace earlier conclusions are treated as first-class scholarly artifacts. A mathematical civilization is not sustained merely by saving documents. It is sustained when future researchers can reconstruct the precise statement, revisit the evidence, inspect the dependencies, reject an invalid inference, and open a better question. title: Calibration, Conformal Uncertainty, and Fairness of Large Language Models for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction after ICU Admission: Evaluation on MIMIC-IV with External Validation on MIMIC-III
abstract: This is a preregistered retrospective, non-interventional prediction-model evaluation using publicly available de-identified ICU data (MIMIC-IV v3.1 and MIMIC-III v1.4). We do not train or fine-tune large language models (LLMs). The study evaluates three axes of LLM-based in-hospital mortality prediction: calibration, conformal uncertainty, and subgroup fairness, with external validation. Structured first-day (0–24 h) ICU features are converted into fixed clinical vignettes. A primary LLM (deepseek-v4.1-flash) outputs an integer probability (0–100) of in-hospital death. Baselines include XGBoost, logistic regression, and SOFA. The confirmatory analysis uses a pilot-excluded cohort (n≈55,223) to avoid bias from previously observed pilot samples (12,000 stratified batch + 200 probe). The full cohort (n≈67,423) is reported as a sensitivity analysis. Primary estimands: (1) calibration via ECE (equal-frequency 10 bins) and calibration slope before/after Platt scaling; (2) conformal prediction using LAC (Least Ambiguous Set-Valued Classifier, Sadinle et al.) with target coverage 90%/95%, reporting empirical coverage and prediction set sizes; (3) subgroup fairness (sex, age, race_group including UNKNOWN_LIKE) via ΔECE and equalized odds gap. External validation applies locked calibration and conformal thresholds from MIMIC-IV directly to mapped MIMIC-III without retraining. Reporting follows TRIPOD+AI. Expected outcomes: a methodological assessment of whether LLM mortality probabilities are well-calibrated, whether LAC provides clinically interpretable uncertainty sets, and whether subgroup disparities exist. Exploratory pilot results (DeepSeek n=12,000; MiMo n=4,000) are disclosed as non-confirmatory and are excluded from the primary analysis. Preregistration lock date: 2026-10-13 (Asia/Shanghai). No institutional PHI; CITI/PhysioNet training completed.

title: Nonlocal effects via local quantum Fisher information: characterizations and interpretations
abstract: Abstract We introduce a quantum Fisher information based measurement-induced nonlocality (QFI-MIN), which quantifies the maximal statistical distinguishability induced by locally invariant unitary dynamics. The proposed measure inherits desirable properties including positivity, local unitary invariance, monotonicity under local operations, and immunity to the local ancilla problem. Analytical expressions are obtained for pure states, arbitrary two-qubit states, and two-qubit X states, revealing a direct connection with entanglement for pure systems. The proposed measure admits direct operational interpretations in local channel discrimination and quantum parameter estimation. Specifically, QFI-MIN quantifies the maximal infinitesimal distinguishability and parameter-estimation sensitivity achievable through locally invariant unitary encodings. Its behavior under amplitude damping, depolarizing, and generalized amplitude damping channels demonstrates robustness against environmental noise. The proposed framework provides an operationally meaningful quantifier of quantum correlations, establishing a direct connection between nonlocality, quantum metrology, and quantum information processing.

title: Federated learning with update level noise perturbation and blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving healthcare ECG classification
abstract: We propose FedChainDP, a federated learning framework that combines update-level noise perturbation with blockchain audit logging for privacy-preserving collaborative ECG classification across multiple healthcare institutions. Healthcare institutions face a fundamental tension: deep learning models require large, diverse training datasets to achieve high diagnostic accuracy, yet strict privacy regulations such as HIPAA and GDPR restrict the sharing of raw patient data across organizational boundaries. FedChainDP resolves this tension by enabling hospitals to collaboratively train a shared CNN model without exchanging raw electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. Each hospital trains locally on its private data and shares only noise-perturbed model updates, to which Gaussian noise is added once per federated round; these updates are encrypted with AES-256-GCM before transmission and logged on an immutable blockchain with Merkle-tree integrity protection and smart-contract policy checks on the reported noise parameters. Because this round-level noise schedule does not satisfy the assumptions of the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, the accountant output for the main configuration (ε_nom = 7.84 at δ = 10⁻⁵) is reported only as a nominal indicator, and no formal (ε, δ)-differential privacy guarantee is claimed. We evaluate FedChainDP on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia dataset partitioned across 5 hospitals using Dirichlet-based non-IID distributions. Our CNN model achieves 98.91% ± 0.14% accuracy under federated learning with update-level noise injection (σ_mult = 1.1), compared to 98.81% ± 0.31% for centralized training and 98.57% ± 0.17% for federated learning without noise-based privacy protection. These accuracies were obtained under a beat-level random split performed after duplication-based class balancing, so duplicated minority-class beats and beats from the same patients can occur in both training and test sets; they therefore reflect performance within this resampled benchmark and do not establish generalization to independent unseen beats or patients. A comprehensive privacy-utility analysis across noise multiplier settings (σ_multiplier ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 100}) demonstrates that classification accuracy remains above 98% across all evaluated noise levels. A black-box membership inference attack achieved 50.28% accuracy (near random guessing) against the noise-perturbed model; however, comparable near-chance accuracy was also obtained against the models trained without noise (49.16% centralized; 49.48% federated), so this result neither isolates a benefit of the noise mechanism nor substitutes for a formal privacy guarantee. A single-machine scalability simulation across 2 to 20 simulated hospitals produced accuracies of 98.90% (2 hospitals), 95.10% (5 hospitals), 93.80% (10 hospitals), and 97.20% (20 hospitals), respectively, while the simulated blockchain audit trail adds negligible overhead (0.059–0.091 s average mining time per block within the single-machine environment). FedChainDP incorporates technical safeguards relevant to healthcare privacy and accountability objectives across four dimensions: multi-technique privacy integration, blockchain-logged policy checks on reported noise parameters, smart contract access control, and empirical membership-inference evaluation.

title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.

title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning
abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.

title: Delegating Earth science model calibration to knowledge-guided LLM agents
abstract: Applying process-based Earth science models to new sites and questions often requires expert calibration decisions. Reliable delegation to language-model agents must preserve scientific competence and reproducibility. Here we develop a general calibration harness (GCH) for end-to-end delegation from a calibration request to assessed results. Constrained by a knowledge infrastructure (KI) and a validation convention, agents define parameter domains, observation mappings and objectives, and generate model-specific code. GCH checks the formulations against the same declarations and freezes them before numerical search and assessment, which require no further agent judgement. Agent-authored workflows executed across six model families, with assessment identifying unmet criteria. In snow-model tests, five of five knowledge-guided specifications executed on the first attempt, compared with none of five given only the model name, achieving validation Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.81-0.94 against 0.57 for defaults. Under a common objective, independent GR4J formulations yielded scores within 0.001 NSE; re-evaluating eleven saved parameter vectors reproduced their metrics. In ten paired VIC tests with matched budgets, fixed search was non-inferior to continuing agent proposals (margin, -0.02 NSE; median difference, -0.003). This separation enables end-to-end calibration delegation with inspectable scientific choices and reproducible numerical evaluation.

title: Collapse, Repair, and Drift: Dissecting Fine Tuning Dynamics in Speech Language Models
abstract: Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is commonly monitored through training and evaluation loss, but loss does not fully characterize how model functionality evolves along the same trajectory. We study this gap through dialect adaptation of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$. Character error rate (CER) reveals pronounced transient collapse and recovery whose severity and temporal structure are only weakly reflected by loss. Bidirectional layer patching reveals strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize during recovery. Pairwise gradient similarity alone does not reliably indicate optimization stability, whereas raw gradient spectral analysis provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization: successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, while failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent fluctuations. Finally, AdamW update transfer bypasses pronounced early collapse, yet substantial Mandarin degradation still emerges later in training. These results motivate three separable SFT dynamics: collapse, repair, and drift, and show that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation.

title: Frequency Routing and Identity Conditioning for Thermal-to-Visible Face Translation
abstract: Thermal-to-visible (T2V) face translation has important applications in nighttime biometric recognition, low-light surveillance, and human interpretation of thermal observations. The task remains challenging because thermal images do not directly record visible appearance, while the cross-spectral cues useful for reconstruction vary across frequency components and semantic roles. Existing spatially conditioned models tend to process these cues through a homogeneous adaptation path and do not explicitly separate local structure from global identity. We propose FreqID-Control, a parameter-efficient framework that organizes thermal guidance according to spectral reliability and semantic role while preserving the pretrained generative prior. It combines frequency-routed low-rank adaptation, which allocates separate transformation subspaces to low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail, with shared cross-spectral identity conditioning, which supplies compact global identity tokens independently of spatial thermal tokens. A controlled analysis on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces provides the empirical basis for this design, revealing stable low-frequency correspondence and edge-localized detail correspondence. Experiments on both datasets demonstrate strong image fidelity and biometric identity preservation, while controlled ablations on MCXFace confirm the complementary contributions of frequency routing and shared identity conditioning.

title: What Information Buys in Active Inference
abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.

title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

title: zPocket: Better Pocket Finding with Frozen Co-Folding Features
abstract: Identifying protein-ligand binding sites (pockets) is important for understanding protein function and developing drugs. However, no public method has leveraged co-folding models for novel pocket prediction; furthermore, this task lacks a suitable benchmark as existing benchmarks are within the training distribution of co-folding models. We therefore developed PocketWatch,a curated dataset of biologically relevant ligand pockets. The PocketWatch test set consists of unseen pockets stratified by sequence similarity, structural similarity, and crypticity to enable evaluation of generalization to novel and challenging pockets. Using this dataset, we develop zPocket, a method that trains pocket-prediction heads on top of frozen features from co-folding models. We show that zPocket heads outperform baseline methods across all stratifications. Our best zPocket model achieves overall per-target AUPRC of 0.745 compared to 0.598 and 0.595 for the strongest baselines, VN-EGNN and UniSite-1D retrained on the PocketWatch split (0.559 and 0.531 when using the published weights); the widely used P2Rank reaches 0.477. We further show that zPocket can be used to outperform baseline methods on top-N+2 recall of predicted pocket centroids through clustering per-residue predictions or using zPocket to rescore centroids proposed by other models. Finally, we explore two applications of zPocket: crystallographic fragment screens and a proteome-scale scan for uncharacterized pockets on human proteins. Together these results suggest that zPocket heads built on co-folding trunk features can greatly advance ligand binding site prediction.

title: Delay Complexity Dimension: Learning with Delayed and Censored Labels
abstract: We study PAC learning of binary classifiers when labels arrive after random delays and are censored beyond an observation window $W$. How many samples does this observation model require? We propose a distribution-dependent answer, the Delay Complexity Dimension (DCD). The DCD combines the VC dimension with the exact label-information rate of the observation channel. Every learner needs $Ω(\mathrm{DCD}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples. An oracle pseudo-label ERM matches this rate on the instance family of the lower bound, up to constants and logarithmic factors. On that family the DCD is within a constant factor of the classical censored-ERM complexity, and whether the DCD rate is achievable where the two separate remains open. The theory also yields a quantization scheme under which delay information lowers the residual label variance, an expedition policy with a $(1-1/e)$ guarantee for its version-space objective, and a phenomenon with no analogue in the no-delay setting. Under a fixed collection horizon, a moderate window can strictly beat immediate labels. Experiments on synthetic data and the Criteo conversion logs support these predictions. A budget-matched test of a companion labeler-diversity prediction is reported as a negative result.

title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.

title: Kolorektal Histopatolojide Tarayıcılar Arası Genellemede Frekans-Farkında Modüller ve Renk Normalizasyonu Stratejileri Gerçekten Katkı Sağlıyor mu? Çok-Tohumlu Bir Değerlendirme
abstract: Dijital patolojide farklı tarayıcıların yol açtığı alan kayması (domain shift), derin öğrenme modellerinin kurumlar arası kullanımını sınırlamaktadır. Bu soruna yönelik iki yaygın strateji — frekans-farkında mimari bileşenler ve normalize edilmemiş veriyle karışık eğitim — literatürde çoğunlukla tek koşumlu deneylerle olumlu sunulmaktadır. Bu çalışmada, kolorektal doku sınıflandırması bağlamında bu stratejilerin güçlü bir evrişimli sinir ağı (ConvNeXt-Small) taban modeline gerçek bir katkı sağlayıp sağlamadığı, üç tohumlu ve dış doğrulamalı kapsamlı bir protokolle sınanmıştır. Modeller NCT-CRC-HE-100K üzerinde eğitilip bağımsız CRC-VAL-HE-7K veri seti üzerinde test edilmiştir. Üç özgün bileşen — tarayıcılar-arası frekans normalizasyonu (CFN), doku-frekans ayrıştırma modülü (TFDM) ve uyarlanabilir füzyon (AFSM) — çıkarmalı (leave-one-out) ablasyonla; karışık ve normalize eğitim ise 2×2 tasarımıyla değerlendirilmiştir. Bulgular tutarlı biçimde olumsuzdur: taban modelin dış doğruluğu (%96.60±0.45), incelenen bileşenlerin hiçbiri eklendiğinde istatistiksel olarak anlamlı biçimde iyileşmemekte; CFN bileşeni dış doğruluğu sistematik olarak düşürmektedir (−0.70 yüzde puanı). Karışık eğitim, normalize eğitime kıyasla yalnızca +0.39 puan fark yaratmakta ve güven aralıkları tümüyle çakışmaktadır; hedeflenen zayıf sınıflarda (STR, MUS) dahi anlamlı iyileşme gözlenmemektedir. Sonuçları büyük ölçüde tohumlar arası varyans (±0.15–1.19 puan; tek-koşum yayılımı 2.2 puana ulaşmakta) belirlemektedir. Çalışma, bu kıyaslama kümesinde küçük mimari ve veri-stratejisi kazanç iddialarının önemli bölümünün tohum gürültüsüyle açıklanabileceğini göstermekte ve tek-koşumlu karşılaştırmalara karşı uyarmaktadır.

title: Weighted Proportional Conflict Redistribution for Heterogeneous LLM Ensembles
abstract: Smaller language models often exhibit high confidence in erroneous predictions, undermining traditional ensemble methods. In heterogeneous ensembles, simple averaging can grant disproportionate influence to overconfident but incorrect outputs. This paper introduces a reliability-weighted extension of the Proportional Conflict Redistribution rule (PCR6), where model-specific weights are derived from validation accuracy. We provide a formal treatment of the conflict measure, prove that the weighted rule avoids Zadeh's paradox in the high-conflict regime, and establish a quasi-associativity bound of order O(K_max²). We further justify linear weighting from both Bayesian (conjugate Dirichlet) and minimax perspectives, and compare the approach with logarithmic pooling and Dirichlet calibration. Empirical evaluation on a multi-model MMLU setting shows that the primary practical benefit of weighted PCR6 in our experiments lies in improved calibration (substantially lower Expected Calibration Error) rather than large accuracy gains over simple averaging. Accuracy improvements appear most plausible when ensemble members differ markedly in reliability; when models are comparably strong, the method remains competitive while producing better-calibrated probabilities. The fusion step itself is computationally lightweight (tens of microseconds per query for small ensembles).

title: dnf-composer: A C++ library and application for building and simulating Dynamic Neural Field architectures
abstract: Dynamic Neural Fields (DNFs) provide a mathematical framework for modeling continuous neural population dynamics that underlie perception, working memory, decision-making, and embodied cognition. **dynamic-neural-field-composer** (dnf-composer) is an open-source C++20 library and interactive application for composing, simulating, and visualizing one- and two-dimensional DNF architectures. ### What this capsule runs The Reproducible Run builds dnf-composer **v2.12.1** from source and runs three headless checks: 1. **Test suite** — the full GoogleTest suite → `results/test-report.xml`, `results/tests.log` 2. **Numerical validation** — 300 one-dimensional simulations (stimulus on for 500 steps, then off for 500 steps), saving activation profiles → `results/validation-1d/` 3. **Benchmark** — headless simulation throughput (steps/s) → `results/timings.csv` The interactive GUI needs a display, so it is not part of the Reproducible Run. Pre-built binaries and documentation: https://github.com/Jgocunha/dynamic-neural-field-composer

evidence.title: dnf-composer: A C++ library and application for building and simulating Dynamic Neural Field architectures
evidence.abstract: Dynamic Neural Fields (DNFs) provide a mathematical framework for modeling continuous neural population dynamics that underlie perception, working memory, decision-making, and embodied cognition. **dynamic-neural-field-composer** (dnf-composer) is an open-source C++20 library and interactive application for composing, simulating, and visualizing one- and two-dimensional DNF architectures. ### What this capsule runs The Reproducible Run builds dnf-composer **v2.12.1** from source and runs three headless checks: 1. **Test suite** — the full GoogleTest suite → `results/test-report.xml`, `results/tests.log` 2. **Numerical validation** — 300 one-dimensional simulations (stimulus on for 500 steps, then off for 500 steps), saving activation profiles → `results/validation-1d/` 3. **Benchmark** — headless simulation throughput (steps/s) → `results/timings.csv` The interactive GUI needs a display, so it is not part of the Reproducible Run. Pre-built binaries and documentation: https://github.com/Jgocunha/dynamic-neural-field-composer

title: Posterior sampling of word embeddings
abstract: Abstract We study Bayesian inference for probabilistic word embedding models, including skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) and continuous bag-of-words (CBoW). These models are widely used for inference, but their posteriors are non-identifiable under general linear transformations, which prevents meaningful Bayesian uncertainty quantification. We provide a simple and principled identifiability constraint that yields a well-defined posterior without altering the data model. Building on this, we develop scalable, fully Bayesian posterior sampling algorithms for SGNS and CBoW using Pólya–Gamma augmentation. Our block Gibbs samplers yield exact samples from the posterior and scale well to large corpora due to their straightforward parallelisation. We discuss the efficient implementation of the Gibbs sampler, and provide a fast TensorFlow reference implementation. In a combination of simulations and empirical experiments, we demonstrate that the sampler is both accurate and computationally efficient. It matches the accuracy of NUTS-HMC at a fraction of the computational cost and avoids the variance underestimation of mean-field variational inference. On large real datasets, we show that posterior means yield improved predictive performance, while posterior credible intervals provide meaningful uncertainty quantification for semantic similarity.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Mineral Prospectivity Mapping with Positive-Unlabeled Learning and Conformal Calibration: Ni Mineralization in the Yilgarn Craton
abstract: Abstract Mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) supports exploration targeting, yet most machine learning approaches emphasize point probabilities with limited uncertainty quantification or coverage guarantees. Regional MPM faces incomplete deposit labels from biased exploration, spatial autocorrelation invalidating random cross-validation, and limited decision-relevant guidance linking probability surfaces to exploration priorities. This study develops a framework that combines positive-unlabeled learning, nested spatial block cross-validation, bootstrap ensemble uncertainty, and cross-conformal calibration, and converts the resulting signals into five priority zones defined by lift-based percentile thresholds and a 30% relative interquartile range ( $$\rho _{\text {IQR}}$$ ρ IQR ) cut-off. On the Yilgarn Craton, Western Australia (70,200 grid cells at 5 km resolution, 818 cells containing at least one known Ni deposit location, a 1.17% positive rate), the framework uses nested fivefold spatial block cross-validation with 50 km blocks informed by an empirical variogram. XGBoost and a BaggingPU-XGBoost variant achieve nearly identical outer test PR-AUC of 0.195 and 0.194 and ROC-AUC of 0.911, and the Excluded zone removes 9% of the positive cells at empirical coverage exceeding the 85% nominal target. BaggingPU-XGBoost produces more stable high-probability predictions, with median $$\rho _{\text {IQR}}$$ ρ IQR of 18% in the top 1% of bootstrap mean probabilities compared with 48% for XGBoost. This stability advantage shifts deposits into a more populated Immediate zone, so the combined Immediate and Priority zones of BaggingPU-XGBoost capture 33% of the positive cells compared with 23% for XGBoost. The framework provides an uncertainty-informed prioritization for MPM workflows in which discovery efficiency must be balanced against costs and investment risks.
