title: Beyond Generation: What a Decision-Native Model Does Well in a Long Task, and What It Needs from Its Harness
abstract: Many automated workflows end in a bounded decision among options that the software already knows, yet such decisions are usually obtained from language models by generating text. Decision-native models instead return one of the supplied options together with a probability distribution. We study one of them, Jev, on the Three-Phase Vault, a puzzle small enough to be solved exactly (65,375 states, a 26-move optimum), so that every step of every run can be scored against the optimum. On 400 fixed states with identical inputs, Jev chose an optimal action more often than three reasoning models (53.0% against 28.5–36.3%), at a median latency of 0.41 seconds against 2.3–4.4 seconds. Over whole runs, however, Jev often undid its own progress and completed 22% of runs under a minimal harness, against 86%, 32% and 26% for the reasoning models. A harness that kept a persistent goal and filtered the options by it raised Jev's completion from 0% to 94% (141 of 150 runs), and replaying the original code three and a half weeks later gave 48 of 50. Small changes then reduced completion sharply: shuffling the order of the options (18 of 50), rewording the goal instruction (32 of 50) and keeping drop actions in the filtered set (4 of 70). On twelve generated environments the filter's gain was not statistically reliable, and removing drop actions, which helped on the Vault, lowered completion there from 73% to 13%. The performance of a decision-native model on a long task thus depends on a harness whose effect is large and fragile, and building harnesses that transfer is the main open problem. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Data, code and all recorded runs: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23323117.

title: Propuesta conceptual de un modelo adaptativo basado en inteligencia artificial para la detección de fraude en transacciones internacionales: innovaciones, riesgos emergentes y aplicabilidad en PYMES de Latinoamérica
abstract: El crecimiento de las transacciones digitales internacionales ha incrementado la exposición de las pequeñas y medianas empresas (PYMES) al fraude financiero, en un contexto en el que la inteligencia artificial (IA) puede emplearse tanto para combatir como para perpetrar este delito. En México, se reportaron pérdidas aproximadas de 17,400 millones de pesos durante el primer semestre de 2025. Este trabajo propone, a nivel conceptual, un modelo adaptativo de detección de fraude bajo la modalidad de Software como Servicio (SaaS) dirigido a PYMES latinoamericanas. Se empleó una metodología mixta de alcance exploratorio-descriptivo, que combinó una revisión documental narrativa, el análisis descriptivo de registros operativos agregados de una organización de remesas (octubre de 2024 a enero de 2025) y el diseño de una arquitectura de entrada, procesamiento y salida de datos. En el caso analizado, 103.720 llamadas fueron derivadas al área de fraude y solo el 33,53 % se confirmó como tal, lo que evidencia la fricción que generan los sistemas basados en reglas fijas. El modelo propuesto combina aprendizaje supervisado, aprendizaje no supervisado y revisión humana, y está diseñado para reducir esa fricción sin descuidar la seguridad. Su desempeño no fue medido en este estudio y requiere validación empírica posterior.

title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.

title: Dataset on genre and news topic persistence between versions 1 and 2 of CLASSLA-web
abstract: The dataset contains metadata on documents from the CLASSLA-web v2 web crawl (http://hdl.handle.net/11356/2079), describing each document by its (1) document identifier, (2) URL, (3) web domain, (4) predicted genre, (5) predicted topic, (6) the length in terms of number of characters and, most importantly, (7) whether the document is considered to have a near-duplicate in the CLASSLA-web v1 corpus collection. This dataset originated from the paper “What Persists across Web Crawls? Genre and News Topic Variation in South Slavic Web Corpora”, accepted for publication at the 13th Web-as-Corpus Workshop (WaC-13), co-located with EMNLP 2026. We make the dataset openly available to facilitate follow-up research on this topic.

title: Exact discrete logarithms from a flagged polygonal transform
abstract: Assume the flagged polygonal-transform and exact-factoring interfaces specified in the paper. We construct a polynomial-time uniform quantum circuit family over one fixed finite gate set that computes discrete logarithms in prime fields with probability one and polynomial worst-case resources. For prime-order inputs, each verified Fourier-bin label has probability at least 1/(81q). Given its verified logarithm, that probability is computable exactly by a bounded number of lattice-point counts in dimension at most thirteen. Dyadic completion produces success probability exactly one quarter, followed by one exact amplification step. All sampled probabilities are dyadic; no input-dependent rotation or postselection is used.

title: When AI Becomes the Travel Agent: How Tourists Negotiate Trust, Autonomy, and Authenticity in AI-Generated Travel Decisions
authors: Fatimah Abdulaziz Alshiha Muhammad Awais Bhatti
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly transforming how tourists search for information, plan itineraries, and make travel decisions. However, limited qualitative research explains how tourists negotiate their agency when AI becomes actively involved in travel decision-making. This study explores how tourists experience GenAI-mediated travel decisions, focusing on autonomy, trust, skepticism, authenticity, and spontaneity. Drawing on a qualitative research approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with six tourists who had experience using GenAI for travel planning. Thematic analysis identified five interconnected themes: AI as a travel decision partner; between convenience and decision autonomy; trust, verification, and skepticism; the tension between ai optimization and travel spontaneity; and reconstructing authenticity in AI-mediated travel. The findings indicate that tourists perceive GenAI as a decision partner rather than a replacement for human judgment. AI enhances planning convenience but can increase reliance, making autonomy a negotiated process. Trust is conditional and supported by verification, while AI optimization creates tensions with spontaneity. Furthermore, AI can facilitate authentic experiences while potentially contributing to algorithmic standardization. The study contributes to tourism research by conceptualizing AI-mediated travel decision-making as a process of negotiated agency between tourists and AI.

title: Multidimensional Evaluation of LLM-Generated MPC Programs
abstract: Large language models can generate programs that compile and pass functional tests, but these outcomes are insufficient for evaluating code in secure multi-party computation (MPC). MPC programs must also follow the target interface's programming constraints, implement the requested algorithm, and satisfy the stated secure-operation efficiency criteria. Using NLMPC, a staged code-generation framework, we conduct an empirical study of 3,600 C++ programs generated by three LLMs for three algorithms under four generation settings that vary API instructions, explicit programming constraints, and iterative repair. We evaluate each program along four dimensions: functional correctness, MPC conformance, algorithmic adherence, and MPC efficiency.

title: Disaggregating artificial intelligence training: a transatlantic framework for copyright and generative AI
abstract: Generative AI disputes are often framed as a single question: whether training a model on copyrighted works is lawful. This article argues that the framing is misleading. AI training is a pipeline that begins with acquisition and preprocessing. It continues through intermediate copying during optimisation, retention and deployment, and each stage raises distinct copyright questions. Recent US decisions diverge in result but share a stage-specific method. Bartz v Anthropic separated transformative optimisation from a pirated library. Kadrey v Meta made market harm turn on evidence. Thomson Reuters v Ross Intelligence rejected fair use where copied editorial content supported a directly competing product. The English High Court’s Getty Images judgment likewise distinguished upstream copying, the legal character of model weights and downstream outputs. Together they support analysis through provenance, purpose and substitution. This article develops that comparative US–UK framework, situates it within the DSM Directive and EU AI Act, and translates it into proposals for pleading, discovery and documentation. It also develops proposals for retention, output controls and remedies. A South Korean survey serves only as contextual evidence of bounded compensation preferences. The central claim is methodological: liability should attach to the relevant operation, copy, actor and territory. The analysis should separately address the resulting market effect rather than ‘training’ in the aggregate.

title: A hierarchical dual-stream POMDP–IPSO framework for multi-UAV cooperative inspection scheduling and control
abstract: Large-scale power-transmission-line inspection requires coordinated task allocation and safe local motion control. This study presents a hierarchical dual-stream partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP)–Improved Particle Swarm Optimization (IPSO) framework for multi-UAV inspection. At the lower level, a centralized-training/decentralized-execution Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) algorithm trains a dual-stream actor that separates short-horizon collision perception from communication-topology coordination; a sigmoid curriculum fuses the streams and a differentiable safety filter enforces soft separation, boundary, velocity, and acceleration constraints. At the upper level, IPSO jointly optimizes task-to-UAV assignment and visit order under time, energy, priority-coverage, battery, and time-window criteria. Closed-loop feedback triggers replanning when tasks are completed, deadlines are threatened, energy reserves are low, or a route segment becomes infeasible. In addition to the restricted operational scenarios, we provide a reproducible benchmark with 19 scenarios, 574 tasks, 30 scheduling seeds, and 30 controller test seeds. Under equal evaluation budgets, IPSO reduced mean fitness by 4.8% relative to standard PSO, while the reconstructed dual-stream MAPPO controller achieved 89.3% ± 10.1% task success. Across the evaluated cases, the proposed framework achieved better average performance in most scenarios rather than uniformly dominating every baseline. The code, generated scenarios, raw run-level data, and 600-dpi figures are supplied for independent reproduction. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
abstract: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

title: DuplexBridge: Coordinating Understanding and Generation for Unified Image Editing
abstract: Complex image editing requires faithful task interpretation and accurate execution, but a failed edit does not reveal which responsibility failed. We present DuplexBridge, which uses a unified model's own understanding capability to enhance prompts for its own generation capability, without an external understanding module. A source-grounded bridge specifies targets, final-state changes, and preservation constraints. Understanding is supervised on fidelity to the original request without observing the generated image; generation is supervised on execution of the condition it actually receives. Reciprocal trust checks selectively admit global task feedback to each role while retaining independently valid local supervision. We introduce CE-Bench, a 1,200-task benchmark measuring joint satisfaction of task-derived change and preservation requirements. Across three model configurations, the full system improves complete compliance over direct editors by 21.75-25.75 percentage points, with gains also observed on KRIS-Bench, RISEBench, ImgEdit, and GEdit-Bench. From a common supervised Wan-Image initialization, gated joint training reaches 77.08% complete compliance, compared with 70.92% without gates and 75.00% when generation-local supervision instead checks the original task with both gates retained. These results support distinct local responsibilities and selective shared feedback for joint understanding-generation adaptation.

title: Agentic-MatriBO: Capability-Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials and Chemical Design
abstract: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation from sequential observations under a limited budget. Large language models can use task knowledge to propose adjustments, but composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. We present Agentic-MatriBO, a capability-compiled agentic Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that represents BO components and selection conditions as composable capabilities. A language policy proposes BO recipes and candidate plans; a compiler checks proposals against the registered capability catalog; and a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates. Oracle observations are stored in research memory and inform later rounds. We compare Agentic-MatriBO with eight baselines on four offline finite candidate pools---COF, PCE10, Buchwald--Hartwig (BH), and Suzuki--Miyaura---using five seeds per condition; results are reported descriptively. Across the four tasks, Agentic-MatriBO has the best mean endpoint quality after orienting each objective so that higher is better. On COF, it reaches the tabulated optimum in all five seeds both in the end-to-end comparison and after shared initialization, where it also retains an advantage in cumulative quality. Its normalized area under the best-so-far quality curve during the BO stage (nAUC-BO) is substantially higher on COF, near parity with the best baseline on PCE10 and BH, and lower on Suzuki. COF ablations show that removing the capability compiler or evidence gate coincides with lower cumulative quality and fewer exact-optimum hits. The framework provides an inspectable interface for evidence-conditioned BO adaptation.

title: ULDA Topological Decoder Engine - Fixed-Point Sexagesimal Architecture
abstract: A fixed-point sexagesimal architecture for radix-drift elimination in 3D spacetime topological quantum error correction simulations. Uses a pure integer register space (Base-60) with dual-register error accounting, eliminating IEEE 754 floating-point roundoff artifacts. Achieves machine-zero convergence (2.62 x 10^-14 at depth r=12).

title: From Circuits to Policies: A Review and Taxonomy of Decision Making and Strategy Selection in LLMs and LLM Agents
abstract: Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.

title: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
abstract: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the standard encoding. Across 13 end-to-end applications in healthcare, graph, and database analytics, HULK improves performance over the arithmetic approach used by prior works by up to 7.26x (CPU) and 6.65x (GPU), and on average by 2.32x/1.78x/1.45x (CPU) and 2.08x/1.70x/1.51x (GPU) for healthcare/graph/database analytics. When we increase the reduction depth in a representative application, HULK's speedup grows to 10.10x over the state-of-the-art GPU baseline.

title: CityCode: Building Agent-Operable 3D Cities from Sparse Aerial Observations
abstract: Urban spatial intelligence calls for 3D cities that agents can measure, interpret, and modify across successive tasks. Maintaining such cities as persistent, code-based states requires lightweight acquisition and support for consistent state updates without repeated dense reconstruction. We therefore formulate a new setting for grounded urban world construction: generating large-scale, instance-level parameterized 3D cities from one low-altitude aerial RGB image per region and known camera parameters, while recovering metrically scaled buildings and explicit road geometry and connectivity. We introduce CityCode, an agent-operable representation that unifies metric geometry, urban topology, visual semantics, and 3D assets through persistent entity identities, with dependency-aware versioned execution for validated updates and historical restoration. We further develop Air2Code to construct this representation by combining visual structure extraction with adapted metric depth estimation. To address occlusion and incomplete coverage, recovered structure and observed appearance guide generative completion and subsequent structure-aware 3D generation for buildings and backgrounds. Experiments on CitySample-Aerial and UrbanScene3D demonstrate substantially more accurate metric structure recovery and superior visual fidelity to the target cities compared with the evaluated baselines. Across 50 task chains of 50 steps each, CityCode supports continued querying, editing, planning, and historical restoration over evolving city states. Together, CityCode and Air2Code turn sparse aerial observations into persistent, agent-operable urban worlds for long-horizon urban spatial intelligence.

title: Executable Prefix Values for Locating Agent Failures
abstract: Work on debugging LLM agents treats the "first mistake" marked by a human or LLM judge as ground truth for where a trajectory failed. We ask whether such labels point at causes or symptoms, and make the distinction executable: we restart the agent from reconstructed intermediate states of a failed trajectory and estimate its prefix value V(h_t), the probability of success from each step, with a certified point of no return (PNR) for a failure. On 150 SWE-bench Verified tasks with two frozen open-weight agents, we build such curves for 47 and 60 failed trajectories and probe every step labeled by four frontier judges under the Traverse rubric. We find that the labels do not mark what a controller needs. Judges of different lineages agree on the exact step in only 21/57 cases, and the newest judges flag mistakes in 8/10 and 10/10 successful runs. For 66% of the labels, the agent's success probability does not drop at the labeled step; only 7/188 answers name the decisive step. Restarting at the measured restart point raises expected success from 0.44 to 0.57 offline, and real restarts confirm the advantage, whereas restarting at a judge's label does not (-0.08 to -0.03). We release our code, curves, and labels.

title: Analisis Sentimen Ulasan Pengguna Aplikasi DSW (Depok Single Window) Di Google Play Store Menggunakan Algoritma K-Means
abstract: Depok Single Window (DSW) is an integrated public service application developed by the Depok City Government, yet public awareness of it remains low, and thousands of user reviews on the Google Play Store still reveal technical issues such as login difficulties, slow loading, non-real-time notifications, and online registration failures. These unstructured reviews make it difficult for administrators to quickly and accurately identify recurring problem patterns. This study aims to implement the K-Means Clustering algorithm to perform sentiment analysis and topic grouping of user reviews, and to identify complaint patterns for measurable technical improvement recommendations. The method applied includes collecting 1.190 review data, text preprocessing, term weighting using TF-IDF, determining the optimal number of clusters using the Elbow Method and Silhouette Score, and clustering with K-Means. The results show that the optimal number of clusters is three (k=3). Cluster 0 represents positive reviews containing user appreciation, Cluster 1 contains neutral or informative reviews on general service usage, while Cluster 2 is dominated by technical complaints such as online registration failures, login difficulties, and CCTV access problems, with the lowest average rating. These findings are expected to help developers and the Depok City Government improve digital public service quality.

title: Automated Mathematics: Verification, Understanding, and Discovery - A Verifiable Geometric and Hybrid Architecture
abstract: Mathematics includes creating concepts, formulating worthwhile questions, exploring examples and conjectures, building theories and models, developing computational methods, and communicating understanding; proof is an essential part of this broader activity. Formal correctness, faithful formalisation, and mathematical understanding are distinct achievements. We develop a framework for reporting them separately in automated mathematics. A publication protocol combines kernel checking, an explicit axiom policy, independent statement comparison, and recorded semantic-alignment judgements. A model of proof transmission measures factorisations by shared proof-term cost and establishes an elementary lower bound on the number of bounded components; its interpretation as human assimilation requires additional behavioural assumptions. On the actual graph of formal proof states, discounted terminal reward equals an exponential transform of shortest proof distance. We give a sufficient condition for optimal greedy guidance and quantify the advantage of supplied intermediate lemmas under an independent per-decision error model, distinguishing rollout counts from computation and including the cost of finding the lemmas. These results motivate, but do not validate, joint optimisation of proof structure and search. We then specify a reproducible protocol for measuring declaration-level reuse, with explicit treatment of namespaces, generated certificates, project boundaries, and observation windows. A reproducible source-level pilot selects twelve directory groups before reference counting and searches 122,458 Lean files. Among 10,461 eligible theorem and lemma names, 36.77\% have an import-reachable mention in another file of the same group and 1.55\% in another group. These are lexical measurements, not kernel dependencies or evidence of mathematical decline. The contribution is a set of precise guarantees, measurement boundaries, and release requirements; it is not a claim that formal verification or reuse statistics resolve the problem of understanding.

title: Design and Implementation of a Unique Elements Finder Using Python Sets
abstract: Unique Elements Finder project is a simple but interesting python project. This project is useful to learn the implementation of set for the purpose of finding unique integers from a list. This is done through the Unique Elements Finder project. In both the field of data analysis and the field of programming, the use of duplicate values often results in redundancy and inefficiency. This project is the solution to the problem identified by using the built-in set data structure in python which automatically removes duplicates and only stores the elements which are unique to the set. This program accepts a list of numbers as input and then converts the list to a set to get the unique numbers in an efficient and concise way. Unlike manual methods this methodology minimises the amount of computational complexity that is involved and ensures processing is finished in a short amount of time even when dealing with extremely large datasets. In the fields of data management, analytics and software development, the project shows how elementary concepts such as sets can be used to produce results that are realistic and applicable to the real world. On top of this, it emphasises the importance of having a deep knowledge of Python’s data structures to be able to solve problems quicker and better.

title: Can Zero-Shot Large Language Models Be Trusted for Credit-Risk Prediction? An Explainability Audit Against LightGBM on Loan Default Data
abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) offer a low-barrier route to credit-risk prediction, but regulated use requires evidence on discrimination, probability reliability, and auditable decision patterns. We compare four open-source LLMs (Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B) with LightGBM on 396,030 U.S. LendingClub loans issued from 2007 to 2016. Treating loans as independent and identically distributed observations from this pooled cross-sectional population, we evaluate every model on the same random 20% holdout. All models receive the same 21 structured predictors and output repayment probabilities. We audit empirical decision patterns with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP); separately, each LLM supplies one context-free positive, negative, or neutral direction per feature, which we treat as its feature-level self-explanation. LightGBM achieved ROC-AUC 0.724, PR-AUC 0.907, and Brier score 0.141, compared with 0.669, 0.880, and 0.204 for the best-discriminating LLM, Gemma-2-9B. An equal-weight LightGBM–Gemma ensemble did not improve any metric. In an eight-cycle SHAP audit, each LLM shared six or seven of LightGBM’s ten most important features; these self-explanations agreed with empirical SHAP directions for only 33–67% of assessable top features, revealing self-explanation unfaithfulness under this directional criterion. A nested four-cycle estimate reproduced every LLM’s top-10 set and nearly identical importance ranks, although small magnitude and distribution shifts were statistically detectable. These results caution against standalone zero-shot LLM use in credit risk and support calibration checks, explainability audits, interpretable benchmarks, and human oversight before deployment.

title: A privacy-preserving federated deep learning framework for real-time fraud detection in decentralized financial systems
abstract: The rapid growth of decentralized financial systems has introduced sophisticated fraud that conventional detection methods struggle to identify, due to fragmented data, strict privacy regulations, and the need for real-time response. This study proposes Federated Differentially Private Fraud Detection (FedDP-FD), a privacy-preserving federated deep learning framework that combines differential privacy with a hybrid long short-term memory graph neural network (LSTM-GNN) for real-time fraud detection in decentralized financial networks. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first works to jointly optimize collaborative privacy-preserving training, temporal-relational fraud patterns, and low-latency inference under the high-throughput and heterogeneous conditions of these networks. Each participant trains a hybrid model locally on private transaction data and shares only differentially private gradients. FedDP-FD employs two bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) layers and two GraphSAGE layers whose embeddings are fused via concatenation and dense layers. With adaptive gradient clipping and Gaussian noise, the framework achieves formal sample-level differential privacy of ( ϵ , δ ) ≈ ( 8.48,1 0 − 5 ) . Knowledge distillation, magnitude-based pruning (30%–40%), and 8-bit quantization enable micro-batch inference with early exits. Experiments on Ethereum, Elliptic, and synthetic datasets yield accuracies of 92.9%–94.5%, F1-scores of 0.637–0.739, and precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) values of 0.695–0.804. Given the severe class imbalance (fraud ratio 1.9%–2.2%), the PR-AUC and low false-positive rate demonstrate practical utility. FedDP-FD thus offers a strong trade-off among detection performance, privacy protection, and computational cost, with potential extensions to healthcare and the Internet of Things (IoT).

title: When More Objectives Make Identification Easier: The Role of Preferences and Feedback
abstract: Best-arm identification (BAI) aims to identify the optimal arm using as few samples as possible. While most existing work focuses on a single objective, many real-world applications involve multiple criteria, which motivates the study of BAI in multi-objective bandits. Intuitively, multi-objective identification seems harder, since the learner must identify optimal arms in a higher-dimensional reward space; however, the additional objectives also provide richer feedback that can reduce the required exploration. In this paper, we characterize when and why multiple objectives can make BAI easier. For Gaussian bandits, we establish a characteristic-time lower bound for fixed-confidence identification that holds uniformly across preference orders. Through explicit comparisons under Pareto, linear, and lexicographic preferences, we reveal three phenomena: (i) identifying a larger optimal set can require fewer samples than identifying a unique optimum; (ii) the advantage of vector feedback over coordinate feedback depends fundamentally on the preference order; and (iii) multi-objective identification can require fewer samples than even the easiest corresponding single-objective problem. Finally, we propose Order-Aware Track-and-Stop (OATS), an algorithm that is correct at any prescribed confidence level and asymptotically matches the lower bound.

evidence.title: When More Objectives Make Identification Easier: The Role of Preferences and Feedback
evidence.abstract: Best-arm identification (BAI) aims to identify the optimal arm using as few samples as possible. While most existing work focuses on a single objective, many real-world applications involve multiple criteria, which motivates the study of BAI in multi-objective bandits. Intuitively, multi-objective identification seems harder, since the learner must identify optimal arms in a higher-dimensional reward space; however, the additional objectives also provide richer feedback that can reduce the required exploration. In this paper, we characterize when and why multiple objectives can make BAI easier. For Gaussian bandits, we establish a characteristic-time lower bound for fixed-confidence identification that holds uniformly across preference orders. Through explicit comparisons under Pareto, linear, and lexicographic preferences, we reveal three phenomena: (i) identifying a larger optimal set can require fewer samples than identifying a unique optimum; (ii) the advantage of vector feedback over coordinate feedback depends fundamentally on the preference order; and (iii) multi-objective identification can require fewer samples than even the easiest corresponding single-objective problem. title: QK-Edit: Revisiting Attention-based Injection in MM-DiT for Image and Video Editing
abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.

title: O‘ZBEK TILIDAGI KO‘P MA’NOLI SO‘ZLARNI AVTOMATIK FARQLASHDA MORFOLOGIK BELGILAR VA KONTEKSTUAL MODELLARNI BAHOLASH METODIKASI
abstract: Mazkur maqolada o‘zbek tilidagi ko‘p ma’noli so‘zlarni avtomatik farqlashda morfologik belgilar va kontekstual til modellarining ta’sirini baholash masalasi o‘rganiladi. O‘zbek tilining agglyutinativ xususiyati, so‘zlarning turli grammatik shakllarda qo‘llanishi hamda leksik ma’noning kontekstga bog‘liqligi mazkur vazifani murakkablashtiruvchi omillar sifatida qaraladi. Tadqiqot doirasida ko‘p ma’noli so‘zlarning kontekstual ma’nosini aniqlashda morfologik axborotning foydasini, kam uchraydigan ma’nolarni farqlash imkoniyatlarini va model natijalarining barqarorligini tekshirishga qaratilgan baholash metodikasi taklif etiladi. Metodika bazaviy kontekstual model, morfologik belgilar bilan boyitilgan model va turli kontekst hajmlaridan foydalanadigan yondashuvlarni qiyosiy tahlil qilishni nazarda tutadi. Ma’lumotlarni belgilash, tajriba to‘plamlarini shakllantirish va natijalarni statistik baholash mezonlari yoritiladi. Maqola o‘zbek tilidagi ko‘p ma’nolilikni avtomatik aniqlash tizimlarini izchil va takrorlanadigan tajribalar asosida baholash uchun metodologik asos yaratishga qaratilgan.

title: JoaoAssalim/wavelet-pooling-audio-deepfake: First Version
abstract: Evaluating Wavelet Pooling over Conventional Pooling in CNNs for Audio Deepfake Detection Official implementation repository containing the source code, training configurations, and experimental evaluation scripts for the research paper: "Evaluating Wavelet Pooling over Conventional Pooling in CNNs for Audio Deepfake Detection". Abstract This project investigates the replacement of conventional pooling layers (AveragePooling and MaxPooling) with a custom Wavelet Pooling strategy based on the Daubechies wavelet family within Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for audio deepfake detection. Filter Supports Evaluated: Twelve Daubechies filter sizes (from db4 to db38) applied at the first decomposition level. Datasets: Benchmarked on the Logical Access (LA) scenarios of the ASVspoof 2019 and ASVspoof 2021 datasets. Acoustic Features: Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC) and Linear Frequency Cepstrum Coefficients (LFCC). Statistical Framework: Rigorous validation across ten distinct random seeds utilizing Autorank (Friedman test and Nemenyi post-hoc analysis). Repository Structure models/: CNN architectures integrated with Wavelet Pooling layers. scripts/: Data preprocessing, acoustic feature extraction, training loops, and performance evaluation pipelines. configs/: Hyperparameters and configuration files. seeds/: Random seed logs and recorded metrics supporting the statistical analysis. title: Post-Training, Finetuning, and Steering:A Field Guide for Curating Training Data
abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.

title: RoboFQE: Rollout-Free Evaluation of Visual Robot Policies from Offline Trajectories
abstract: Evaluating robot policies before deployment typically requires producing new trajectories through real-world execution, simulators, or learned world models. These rollout-based approaches impose infrastructure requirements; simulator and world-model evaluators additionally face prediction errors that can compound over the evaluation horizon. In this paper, we study off-policy evaluation as an alternative to rollout-based robot-policy evaluation methods. Specifically, we introduce RoboFQE, an evaluator that estimates the discounted expected return of a target policy from offline robot trajectories without estimating a behavior-policy density, combining fitted Q-evaluation with a pretrained vision foundation model and learned terminal success annotation to bridge the gap between standard OPE benchmarks and continuous-control visual manipulation. Controlled experiments across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that RoboFQE produces accurate discounted-return estimates and preserves policy rankings even on long-horizon manipulation tasks where video world-model evaluators are degraded by autoregressive prediction errors. Ablation experiments show that pretrained vision encoders substantially outperform from-scratch alternatives, particularly on long-horizon tasks, and that learned terminal success annotation enables evaluation without ground-truth reward labels with only slight reduction of accuracy.

title: Detecting Unreliable Classifications from Quantized Models
abstract: Post-training INT8 quantization is typically validated by checking accuracy retention, which requires ground-truth labels often unavailable in low-resource clinical settings. We show a label-free alternative: comparing a model's own output before and after quantization. We compute cosine similarity between the FP32 and INT8 models' output probability vectors for each prediction, which requires only a single forward pass. This output-agreement similarity separates lower-accuracy predictions across four evaluated architectures (ResNet-50, VGG-16-BN, Wide ResNet-50, and ViT-B/16) under fixed-percentile splits, outperforming a confidence-only baseline for all four. These results show that quantized models can be compared to their baselines to assess their drift and determine whether they are well suited for clinical deployment.

title: Probing the Geometry of Color Representations in Multilingual Language Models
abstract: Do multilingual language models learn a universal internal geometry for color, and is it perceptually grounded or primarily linguistic? We decompose color representations into two geometric axes: (P1) alignment to perceptual color space, and (P2) cross-lingual symmetry. Analyzing layerwise embeddings across models and multilingual datasets, we find that perceptual grounding is weak: alignment to CIE-LAB peaks in intermediate layers, then collapses toward output layers. Cross-lingual symmetry degrades with depth, suggesting later layers encode language-specific structure. Functionally, we show that geometric properties predict task performance: models achieve 96.7% accuracy on color classification at layers where P1 alignment peaks, with P1 alignment (r=0.70) significantly correlating with downstream capabilities. Our results reveal a dissociation: text-only LMs learn universal color-language geometry, not universal color-perception geometry, providing diagnostics for where perceptual structure is preserved in language models.

title: Benchmarking and Training Reward Models for Cross-Source Evidence Grounding in Search Agents
abstract: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.

title: SSEmb: Training a Generalizable Speech Retrieval Model Using Only Automatic Speech Recognition Data
abstract: End-to-end speech-to-text retrieval is becoming an important capability for voice agents, allowing spoken queries to retrieve relevant documents without intermediate transcription. Training these retrievers typically depends on large collections of spoken query-document pairs that are costly to acquire and difficult to extend across domains and languages. We introduce \ours, which replaces such task-specific supervision with speech-transcript pairs from standard ASR corpora. A lightweight adapter projects the output of a frozen speech encoder into the retrieval space of a frozen pretrained text embedding model. \ours is competitive with cascaded ASR-then-retrieve systems while reducing inference latency, and outperforms existing publicly available speech embedding models. It also transfers to text-to-speech and speech-to-speech retrieval without additional training. Controlled analyses validate the speech-transcript alignment paradigm, demonstrating robustness to reduced training data and consistent gains from larger corpora. Further ablations of loss functions and trainable modules establish practical guidelines for the framework. Model weights and codes are to be released.

title: Code and analysis pipeline: A kidney-brain-axis machine-learning framework for predicting 28-day mortality in chronic kidney disease with acute brain injury
abstract: Complete analytical pipeline for the study deriving and externally validating a kidney-brain-axis machine-learning framework for 28-day mortality prediction in chronic kidney disease with acute brain injury (CKD+ABI). Contents:- sql/ : SQL extraction scripts for MIMIC-IV v3.1 and eICU-CRD v2.0- python/ : model training, SHAP interpretability, CKD-BI bedside-score derivation, LASSO-logistic nomogram and external-validation code- figure_scripts/ : scripts that regenerate all 10 manuscript figures (Fig. 1-6 and Fig. S1-4) Data availability: MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD are credentialed-access datasets available from PhysioNet (https://physionet.org) after completion of the CITI training course and a formal data use application. These data are governed by the PhysioNet Data Use Agreement and are therefore not redistributed in this deposit; no patient-level data are included. Requirements: Python 3.13 with scikit-learn, XGBoost, SHAP, lifelines and matplotlib (see requirements.txt). Set the environment variable CKD_ABI_DATA_DIR to the directory containing 02_CSV_Data/ and 04_Analysis_Results/ before running the scripts.

title: Non-Blocking Photonic Entanglement Routing and Physical-Layer Deterministic Interlocks for Distributed Quantum Data Centers: Scaling Willow-Class Modular Cryostats via the PHOENIX_BRIDGE Fabric
abstract: Abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) beyond monolithic dilution cryostats demands distributed architectures connecting hundreds of discrete QPUs across a quantum data center fabric. While point-to-point electro-optic links such as PHOENIX_BRIDGE resolve the single-vessel cryogenic cooling bottleneck (15 mK thermal saturation), multi-cryostat clustering faces a severe networking dilemma: conventional quantum repeater architectures rely on matter-based quantum memories that introduce severe decoherence (T2), cryogenic I/O congestion, and non-deterministic queuing latencies. Furthermore, exposing intra-data-center quantum optical channels to external multiplexers creates catastrophic physical-layer vulnerability to state exfiltration and covert decoherence sabotage. This monograph establishes a unified, physical-layer networking architecture for planetary-scale quantum data centers: (1) PHOENIX_ROUTER, a strict-sense non-blocking multi-stage optical switching fabric constructed from sub-nanosecond thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) and barium titanate (BTO) Mach-Zehnder interferometers, executing zero-buffer cut-through entanglement distribution at 1550 nm; (2) a dynamic Cut-Through Entanglement Swapping Protocol that eliminates quantum memory dependencies by synchronizing Bell-state measurements (BSM) directly on flying photonic states, achieving an end-to-end distributed Bell fidelity FBell >= 0.978 with latency under 2.2 microseconds; and (3) a Physical-Layer Determinism Firewall (DFW) that continuously executes real-time Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) Bell tests to detect channel tampering, driving an electro-optic Pockels shutter in < 8 ns to physically isolate compromised cryostats. We derive the non-blocking permutation group theorems, optical Hamiltonian dissipation dynamics, and corporate board liability alignments under the Delaware Caremark Standard, establishing a verifiable blueprint for secure, distributed quantum infrastructure.

This monograph establishes a unified, physical-layer networking architecture for planetary-scale quantum data centers: (1) PHOENIX_ROUTER, a strict-sense non-blocking multi-stage optical switching fabric constructed from sub-nanosecond thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) and barium titanate (BTO) Mach-Zehnder interferometers, executing zero-buffer cut-through entanglement distribution at 1550 nm; (2) a dynamic Cut-Through Entanglement Swapping Protocol that eliminates quantum memory dependencies by synchronizing Bell-state measurements (BSM) directly on flying photonic states, achieving an end-to-end distributed Bell fidelity FBell >= 0.978 with latency under 2.2 microseconds; and (3) a Physical-Layer Determinism Firewall (DFW) that continuously executes real-time Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) Bell tests to detect channel tampering, driving an electro-optic Pockels shutter in < 8 ns to physically isolate compromised cryostats. We derive the non-blocking permutation group theorems, optical Hamiltonian dissipation dynamics, and corporate board liability alignments under the Delaware Caremark Standard, establishing a verifiable blueprint for secure, distributed quantum infrastructure.

title: Weakly Supervised Learning: Toward Robust and Scalable Cancer Pathology Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Artificial intelligence models are increasingly being developed for cancer diagnostics, leveraging digital pathology slides alongside clinical and molecular data to characterize disease features at the patient level and support faster diagnosis and treatment planning. Current model-training approaches rely on detailed annotations of disease features in training data, leaving the vast reservoir of routine clinical data underutilized. Weakly supervised learning (WSL) is a machine learning framework that trains models using coarse or incomplete labels for medical images, rather than requiring detailed annotations specifying the precise locations of target features. This viewpoint argues that WSL should be more widely adopted for developing future oncological pathology models because it reduces dependence on detailed manual annotation. This can substantially expand the pool of data available for model development. When combined with reliable label extraction, appropriate model design, and rigorous validation, such expansion may improve performance across diverse patient populations and facilitate scalable model development. Since WSL can learn associations between image- or patient-level labels and tissue representations of the pathological target without requiring exhaustive spatial annotations, it may help identify candidate morphological features associated with cancer phenotypes and therapeutic outcomes. Such model-derived associations require independent validation before they can be interpreted as clinically useful indicators. A further advantage is that certain WSL frameworks, particularly multiple instance learning approaches employing appropriate instance-selection strategies, can focus model decision-making on diagnostically informative tissue regions. By reducing reliance on irrelevant (noisy) or misleading (spurious) features, these approaches may improve model robustness. With rigorous external validation, WSL could accelerate the development of scalable computational pathology systems with potential clinical utility in cancer healthcare.

title: Programs and data for "An independent certified computation excluding four mutually unbiased bases in dimension six"
abstract: This package contains the programs of the computation described in the paper "An independent certified computation excluding four mutually unbiased bases in dimension six", the logs of every process of the computation and the logs of the earlier execution of Section 3.1, the record files of the atlas, of the mid and fine levels and of the fallback refinement, the list of seed centers, the SHA-256 digests of the executables and of the record files, the difference between the interval arithmetic of the two executions, the commands of the computation and the counts of its tests of Condition (B), the programs, outputs and reports of the checks described in Section 5 of the paper, and the logs of the two trials of Remark 4.2, which are not part of the computation. With this computation, and under the assumption that the machine on which it ran carried out binary64 arithmetic correctly (made precise in Section 3.1 of the paper), the paper shows that there are no four mutually unbiased bases in ℂ⁶. Section, statement and table numbers are those of the paper. The method is the discretization proof of OpenAI's preprint "The maximum number of mutually unbiased bases in dimension six" (24 September 2026), and the programs were written from its text. They evaluate the inequalities of that preprint and of Appendices A and B of the paper, which state where the paper's versions differ from the preprint: three results of the preprint that the programs use are formulated for the programs of the preprint (the bound on the center correction in its Lemma 4.9, the threshold search of its Lemma 5.4 and the graph search of its Lemma 6.8), and for each of them the paper states and proves the version that holds for these programs (Lemmas A.1, A.2 and B.1). The README gives, for each statement of the paper that rests on the computation, the program, the command, the stored output and the running time, and a sample rerun with its log. Requirements: a C++17 compiler (the computation used g++ 13.3.0 on x86-64 Linux, and the build script reproduces the executables of the earlier execution byte for byte with that compiler); Python 3.12 with NumPy; for the checks and the controls also mpmath 1.4, python-flint 0.8 (Arb), SciPy 1.18 and NetworkX 3.6; FLINT 3.3.1 for the C++ checkers of Stages B and C; PARI/GP 2.17.3 for one check. The archive mub6-certified-data.zip (508,337,766 bytes; SHA-256 5a8141210cca669b8c7f356c60433b267fceec1eb407b7dfc8994b7e780b24a9) is stored here in 21 parts, mub6-certified-data.zip.part00 to part20; the command cat mub6-certified-data.zip.part* > mub6-certified-data.zip joins them (HOW-TO-JOIN.txt also gives the Windows command).

title: Agronomic Characterization and Time-Series UAV Phenotyping to Support Field Pea Breeding in Iowa
abstract: Field pea has gained interest in the Midwest U.S. and has the potential to benefit Iowa cropping systems. This study evaluated 17 accessions and 7 Canadian varieties for agronomic and seed yield performance. This study found that PI accession trials exhibit genetic diversity in phenology and canopy traits, whereas the Canadian elite varieties demonstrated great yield potential under Iowa conditions. The accession genotypes matured between 75 DAP (late June) and 95 DAP (late July) across six site-years. The top-yielding Canadian varieties averaged 1961 kg/ha across two site-years. To comprehensively assess field pea performance, this study extracted time-series Unmanned Aerial Vehicle(UAV)-derived traits, assessed UAV-derived traits, and evaluated their correlations with multiple agronomic traits and yield. The results found that UAV-derived time-series canopy area was the most yield-relevant trait (r = 0.63) among all UAV-derived canopy features, vegetation indices, and manually collected measurements. Compared with yield, UAV-derived canopy area showed higher selection reliability (H2 = 0.87, CV = 13.46%), making it suitable for phenotypic selection and accelerating Midwest field pea breeding programs. This study identifies useful UAV-derived features for pea breeding and demonstrates the value of integrating diverse germplasm, elite commercial varieties, and time-series UAV phenotyping. Combining genetic variation from the accession trial with the yield potential of high-performing commercial varieties provides valuable breeding materials and phenotyping strategies for developing locally adapted, high-yielding field pea varieties for future production in the Midwest.

title: The Many Morals of AI: The cautionary bias of North American news narratives in global perspective
abstract: The stories told about artificial intelligence (AI) play a central role in shaping public understanding, policy debates, and expectations about technological change. News media are especially influential in this process. Using a cross-regional corpus of 12,924 English-language news articles about AI published since 2022, we examine how storytelling about AI varies across media systems in four regions: North America, China, India, and the Middle East. Leveraging large language models, we extract the implicit narrative lessons conveyed by each article---commonly known as story morals---capturing value-laden interpretations that extend beyond thematic content or sentiment. We find that North American AI coverage is uniquely characterized by narratives of caution, while under-emphasizing narratives of innovation and collaboration that are more prevalent elsewhere. However, this pattern is largely explained by a broader regional negativity bias in North American news sentiment, rather than by heightened concern about AI itself. Our findings bring into view the culturally conditioned nature of AI news narratives.

title: AssetForge: Asset-Augmented Task Synthesis for Business Automation Agents
abstract: Training business automation agents requires executable tasks that connect a natural-language request to an application state and a verifiable end state. Traditional Rubrics requires Authors to recreate application interfaces, initial records, policy evidence, and outcome checks for each task, entangling business logic with repeated infrastructure work. We introduce AssetForge, an asset-augmented task-construction pipeline that pairs a reusable construction-asset library with task-specific Rubrics. The assets provide application interfaces, world-state components, policy/evidence carriers, and native assertion definitions; the Rubric directs their instantiation for a particular business task. Executable checks and an additional model-based review validate each candidate, return targeted feedback, and support bounded repair before acceptance. On AutomationBench v1.0.6 public-600, fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 6,000 AssetForge examples yields 41.17% on the official strict pass@1 metric, 4.4 times the 9.33% base score (+31.83 points). With the same backbone and GLM-5.3 supervision, AssetForge reaches 41.17% versus 30.33% for traditional Rubrics, a 10.84-point gain (35.7% relative) at the same accepted-example scale (6,000 versus 6,000 examples). Both DeepSeek- and GLM-supervised AssetForge models improve AppWorld completion over the base model on Test-Normal and Test-Challenge. These results establish the advantage of AssetForge's complete construction pipeline on AutomationBench public: the coupled asset-Rubric interface directs Authors toward business logic, while executable checks and model-based review validate their tasks.

title: Uncertainty Evaluation: Bridging Machine Learning and Measurement Science
abstract: Reliable uncertainty evaluation is essential for assessing the trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions, particularly in safety-critical applications. This paper explores conceptual analogies between uncertainty evaluation in ML and measurement science, drawing on the evolution of metrology from error-based approaches to the framework established by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between process-level and result-level quality and to the limitations of the conventional classification of ML uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. It is argued that this dichotomy, similarly to the traditional distinction between random and systematic measurement errors, is inherently model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty evaluation framework. Further analogies between machine learning and measurement field of knowledge are identified concerning distribution shifts, anomalous operating conditions, and the validity of uncertainty evaluation. Building on the proposed considerations, the paper advocates a metrology-inspired approach based on the systematic identification, quantification, and propagation of uncertainty contributions. By extending the methodology already established in measurement science to ML, this approach could offer a potentially rigorous, consistent, and transferable framework for evaluating the trustworthiness of individual predictions.

title: Expression, Verification, and the Scarcity of Aesthetic Education: Reinterpreting Moral Rights in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: This paper argues that the denial of copyright and moral rights to works substantially shaped by human expressive judgment in generative AI systems produces two interrelated harms: the incentive to conceal AI involvement (“trace forgery”) and the proliferation of low-quality content (“flooding”). Drawing on R. G. Collingwood’s distinction between craft and expression in The Principles of Art, it contends that generative AI separates technical execution (craft) from the human process of clarifying an initially indeterminate intention (expression). Chinese judicial practice, which requires process records of prompting, iteration, selection, and modification, already partially recognizes this separation. In the AI era, the functions of moral rights shift: the right of attribution becomes a declaration of authorial acceptance or verification, while the right of integrity protects the author’s evaluative standard and associated reputation. Recognition of these functions aligns incentives toward the production of excellent works and open acknowledgment of AI participation, rather than concealment or flooding. The stakes are uniquely high because the present generation of children is forming aesthetic judgment precisely when craft and expression have been decoupled; the window for correct training of expressive capacity is therefore the true cost of inaction. Historically, copyright has regulated successive scarcities (books, authors, channels, attention), yet its underlying object has always been educational opportunity. The current scarcity is that of proper aesthetic education itself.

title: SteerCA: reinforcement learning environments for controlling cellular automata
abstract: SteerCA is a framework of reinforcement learning environments in which an agent steers a cellular automaton by acting on the cell it stands on, racing the automaton's own dynamics. Every action costs automaton time, so the cost of acting is a continuous difficulty axis set by construction. This release contains the Firebreak forest-fire suite (batched GPU environments in TorchRL, a barrier planner as the reference, and planted instances with certified optima), PPO/A2C/SAC training, paired evaluation, an API for building new automata, and the scripts that regenerate every figure and table of the accompanying papers. The trained policies and training logs are archived separately: 10.5281/zenodo.23328417.

title: Introduction
abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing what it means to lead, and it is doing so quietly, working on how a leader reasons and how decisions get made before anyone quite notices. Leaders who treat it as one more tool to pick up and set down tend to underestimate it badly. This chapter sets out working definitions of leadership and artificial intelligence and places both inside the longer history of how earlier breakthroughs unsettled the people in charge. That history produces the framework the rest of the book is built on: three roles AI can play inside an organization, running from an obedient tool through a working collaborator to an autonomous agent. The chapter also explains why the argument draws on several disciplines at once and how the book’s four parts fit together, from foundations in leadership theory and AI literacy through the daily practice of leading with AI to the institutional questions of strategy, ethics, and governance and finally to extended cases and the decade ahead. One thread runs the whole length: four attributes that have marked capable leaders for as long as anyone has studied them, namely integrity, vision, emotional intelligence, and adaptability.

title: An improved binary arithmetic optimization algorithm with synchronous strong guidance for high-dimensional feature selection
abstract: To address the high redundancy and excessive dimensional issues of high-dimensional data, an improved binary arithmetic optimization algorithm with synchronous strong guidance (SSG-BSIAOA) is proposed. Firstly, to increase the diversity of exploration and the richness of decision-making directions, a bidirectional probability selection strategy is proposed. Then, a trigonometric function factor strategy with eight trigonometric function factors are respectively used to replace the fixed constants so as to increase the algorithm diversity. To improve the insufficient optimization ability of the wrapper method, a synchronous strong guidance strategy based on mutual information and ReliefF dual indicators is proposed, which explores high-quality candidate features from multiple perspectives and breaks through the limitations of single-index evaluation. In the experimental part, the effectiveness of the bidirectional probability selection strategy and the trigonometric function factor strategy is verified through CEC-2022 benchmark functions, and it is proved that the sec-IAOA algorithm is the best variant. Then the performance of the SSG-BSIAOA is verified through 21 high-dimensional UCI datasets, proving the advantages of the proposed method in fitness, accuracy and dimension compression ability. Then, SSG-BSIAOA is applied to 18 micro-array datasets. By comparing with 9 algorithms, it is found that the SSG-BSIAOA has strong optimization ability, good stability, high accuracy and feature simplification. Finally, non-parametric statistical tests, including direct paired Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons with Holm correction, were conducted to further assess the robustness of the observed performance differences.

title: A quantum-assisted latent surrogate model for Bayesian inversion of heterogeneous material properties on NISQ hardware
abstract: Bayesian inversion is widely used in engineering applications, including material characterisation, structural damage identification, and medical diagnostics. These inverse problems are typically ill-posed, because localised variations in material properties must be inferred from noisy observations, and they are computationally intensive, since they often require many evaluations of a high-fidelity forward solver. Quantum computing has recently attracted considerable interest, partly because some near-term algorithms are feasible on NISQ hardware. In particular, PQC combined with classical optimisation enable a hybrid quantum-classical surrogate model. A central obstacle to applying such circuits to inversion is that the discretised parameter and response fields are far too high-dimensional to be embedded in a near-term quantum register. In this work we propose a quantum-assisted latent surrogate model for the Bayesian inversion of inhomogeneous material properties, in which latent compression bridges these high-dimensional fields and the small registers accessible to near-term circuits. The low intrinsic dimensional structure of the spatially varying conductivity and potential fields is exploited by reducing the conductivity through PCA and the response through a convolutional autoencoder. A PQC is then trained to map the latent conductivity to the latent response, and stochastic variational inference is performed entirely in latent space. The methodology is demonstrated on one- and two-dimensional inverse problems under both informative and non-informative priors. evidence.title: A quantum-assisted latent surrogate model for Bayesian inversion of heterogeneous material properties on NISQ hardware
evidence.abstract: Bayesian inversion is widely used in engineering applications, including material characterisation, structural damage identification, and medical diagnostics. These inverse problems are typically ill-posed, because localised variations in material properties must be inferred from noisy observations, and they are computationally intensive, since they often require many evaluations of a high-fidelity forward solver. Quantum computing has recently attracted considerable interest, partly because some near-term algorithms are feasible on NISQ hardware. In particular, PQC combined with classical optimisation enable a hybrid quantum-classical surrogate model. A central obstacle to applying such circuits to inversion is that the discretised parameter and response fields are far too high-dimensional to be embedded in a near-term quantum register. In this work we propose a quantum-assisted latent surrogate model for the Bayesian inversion of inhomogeneous material properties, in which latent compression bridges these high-dimensional fields and the small registers accessible to near-term circuits. The low intrinsic dimensional structure of the spatially varying conductivity and potential fields is exploited by reducing the conductivity through PCA and the response through a convolutional autoencoder. A PQC is then trained to map the latent conductivity to the latent response, and stochastic variational inference is performed entirely in latent space. The methodology is demonstrated on one- and two-dimensional inverse problems under both informative and non-informative priors. We further evaluate the model on IonQ simulator and Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q, and use a lightweight learned denoising stage that recovers the noiseless accuracy to within a small residual. (The abstract has been shortened to meet arXiv's 1,920-character limit. For the full Abstract, please download the full Article.)

title: Gaussian entanglement and quantum communication: geodesic optimization and multimode bounds
abstract: Loss and noise limit the use of light to distribute entanglement, transmit quantum information, and establish secret keys. Gaussian states have a compact description in terms of means and covariance matrices, but their entanglement still requires global optimization. We develop a framework for computing Gaussian-restricted versions of the relative entropy of entanglement and Rains entanglement. An integral representation reveals a convex geometry under matrix geometric means and reduces Gaussian Rains entanglement to relative entropy minimized over Gaussian states with positive partial transpose. We obtain unique optimal reference states and additivity for independent Gaussian input states. Our convex-majorization algorithm has an explicit geometric convergence rate, uniform in the faithful regularization parameter and valid for pure input states. Controlled numerical integration and approximate convex subproblem solutions give a bit-complexity bound that is polynomial in accuracy bits for each fixed rational input covariance matrix, with explicit dependence on covariance size. These calculations bound extractable entanglement and, through the relative entropy of entanglement, extractable secret key. Teleportation simulation, energy allocation, and a convex optimization of passive-basis loss cores give bounds on quantum and private communication under an input-energy constraint, allowing arbitrary two-way classically assisted protocols. Two- and three-mode examples compare the bounds with achievable rates, including matching pure-loss benchmarks. Finally, we separate the Gaussian-restricted quantities from their unrestricted counterparts and give a photon-number truncation method with controlled error for computing the latter.

title: WAVE-0: Bridging VLA Policies and WAMs with Lightweight Latent Future Prediction
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of π_{0.5} from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.

title: CALM: Decentralized Control of Cooperative Aerial Manipulation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Cooperative aerial manipulation is difficult under wind, payload motion, and noisy goal broadcasts because multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are coupled through a shared payload. We present CALM (Cooperative Aerial Learned Manipulation), a decentralized controller for aerial manipulators carrying a basket while tracking a moving ground robot. CALM combines a parameter-shared Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policy, trained using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), with goal estimation, per-UAV Extended State Observers (ESOs), basket-mass estimation, and anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward. The anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward uses estimated goal motion to rotate the formation before position error develops, reducing basket-yaw lag without adding net commanded force. A disturbance-conditioned critic supports centralized training while execution remains decentralized. Across held-out trajectories, CALM achieves lower mean position and orientation errors than all evaluated baselines, including the matched arm baseline (7.68 versus 10.95 cm and 3.3 versus 4.7$^\circ$), the cable-suspended realization, and two model-based controllers. Under unseen full-information-path degradation, CALM remains statistically comparable or superior to the arm baseline. Videos are available at https://petreric.github.io/CALM/.
