title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking Data
abstract: Overview This repository contains the complete data generated from executing a suite of benchmarks on multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) from different hardware providers and technologies. It includes the raw and processed results, and also every quantum circuit, compilation/transpilation setting and execution configuration used. With these, every experiment can be fully reproduced, audited, or re-run on other devices. Its aim is to provide an open, transparent and reproducible basis for comparing the performance of current quantum hardware. Current contents (version [1.0.0]) This version contains the data for the following benchmark: [ghz-benchmarking.zip] (Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services): This version contains the data from benchmarking ten commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of GHZ states via direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state compatible with the genuine multipartite entanglement threshold F = 1/2. All experiments were run through the providers’ cloud services, using each provider’s default compilation and no error mitigation, so the results reflect the performance experienced by end users. File structure Each benchmark is provided as a separate ZIP archive ([benchmark_name].zip). A README.md file in each ZIP describes the formats, naming conventions and data schema for each benchmark. Future versions This is a living dataset. Data from additional benchmarks run on the same and on further devices will be added in future versions of this record. How to cite If you use this dataset, please cite [the associated paper: Authors, Title, arXiv:XXXX.XXXXX] and this dataset. Cite the version-specific DOI to reference the exact data you used, or the concept DOI to reference the dataset as a whole. Acknowledgements

title: CHIMA: Design and Evaluation of a Lightweight Cryptographic System for IoT Applications
abstract: Resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices motivate the investigation into cryptographic designs with measurable implementation costs. This work presents CHIMA (Cryptography cHaotic lIghtweight systeM and Authentication), an experimental system combining a key generator based on chaotic states, a Feistel cipher using the AES substitution box and a keyed bit permutation, and a Lesamnta-LW-based ciphertext check. Logistic, H’enon, and Lorenz systems are examined for key generation, and cipher variants with 64-bit and 128-bit blocks are evaluated. The study reports functional tests, avalanche measurements, NIST statistical tests, and implementation measurements on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M33, and Cortex-M7 microcontrollers. Controlled WiFi/MQTT and LoRa experiments assess communication interoperability. The results show that the chaotic key generator achieved high entropy and passed all NIST statistical tests, indicating its suitability for generating pseudorandom sequences. Based on the combined encryption and decryption times, CHIMA-64 requires 57.95–64.16% less time than PRESENT, while CHIMA-128 requires 23.60–59.36% less time than AES-128 and 13.32–47, as well as 10% less time than CLEFIA across the three platforms.

title: Comparison of Internal Validation Strategies for Estimating Machine Learning Model Performance in One-Year Mortality Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
abstract: Background: Machine learning (ML) performance estimates in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) may depend on internal validation strategy, especially in small datasets. Aim: To develop models for one-year mortality prediction and compare performance, calibration, decision-analytic performance, and uncertainty estimates using a conventional train–test split and nested cross-validation (nCV). Methods: We analyzed a public dataset of 165 patients with HCC, including 63 one-year deaths. Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, and CatBoost were developed using fold-specific preprocessing, cost-sensitive learning, Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization, and training-based threshold selection. L2-penalized logistic regression provided a conventional benchmark. Models were evaluated using a stratified 80/20 split and five-fold nCV with five inner folds. Six stratified splits assessed partition variability, and unweighted models assessed the effect of class weighting. Discrimination, threshold-dependent classification, calibration, and decision-analytic performance were assessed using ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, balanced accuracy, Matthew’s correlation coefficient, Brier score, calibration curves, and decision-curve analysis. Confidence intervals used 2000 bootstrap resamples; SHAP was used for interpretation. Results: In the conventional split, RF and CatBoost achieved the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.892 each), while RF achieved the highest PR-AUC (0.860). Under nCV, RF had the highest mean outer-fold ROC-AUC (0.788) and pooled out-of-fold ROC-AUC (0.784). XGBoost had the highest mean PR-AUC (0.673), whereas CatBoost had the highest pooled PR-AUC (0.648). RF had the lowest mean Brier score (0.188), followed by XGBoost (0.194) and CatBoost (0.203). Calibration varied across models, with pooled calibration slopes of 1.438, 0.691, and 0.427, respectively. Across six 80/20 splits, mean ROC-AUC values were 0.792, 0.769, and 0.761 for RF, XGBoost, and CatBoost, respectively, with substantial partition-dependent variation. Removing class weighting yielded broadly comparable performance. evidence.title: Comparison of Internal Validation Strategies for Estimating Machine Learning Model Performance in One-Year Mortality Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
evidence.abstract: Background: Machine learning (ML) performance estimates in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) may depend on internal validation strategy, especially in small datasets. Aim: To develop models for one-year mortality prediction and compare performance, calibration, decision-analytic performance, and uncertainty estimates using a conventional train–test split and nested cross-validation (nCV). Six stratified splits assessed partition variability, and unweighted models assessed the effect of class weighting. Discrimination, threshold-dependent classification, calibration, and decision-analytic performance were assessed using ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, balanced accuracy, Matthew’s correlation coefficient, Brier score, calibration curves, and decision-curve analysis. Confidence intervals used 2000 bootstrap resamples; SHAP was used for interpretation. Results: In the conventional split, RF and CatBoost achieved the highest test-set ROC-AUC (0.892 each), while RF achieved the highest PR-AUC (0.860). title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Full classification of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard codes
abstract: The $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive codes are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}^n$. A $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard (GH) code is a GH code over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ which is the Gray map image of a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive code. A recursive construction gives such codes $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$, of type $(n;t_1,\dots,t_s)$ and length $p^t$, and a partial classification of them is known. In this paper, we complete the classification of these codes for every prime $p$. The main tool is the derived code, obtained by puncturing the code outside a block of coordinates determined by its kernel. For a nonlinear code $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$ with $t_1\geq2$, the derived code is a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{s-1}}$-linear GH code of the same family, although the mechanism for odd $p$ differs from the binary one. As a consequence, for $t\geq3$, there are $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)$ nonequivalent such codes of length $p^t$ if $p$ is odd, and $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)-1$ if $p=2$, where $\mathcal P(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$. In particular, this completes the classification of the $\mathbb{Z}_{2^s}$-linear Hadamard codes. We also prove a conjecture on the codes with $t_1\geq2$ and $t_s=0$.

title: LegalRewardBench: Benchmarking Reward Models for Legal Preference Evaluation
abstract: Reward models are central to preference alignment for legal tasks, yet existing reward model benchmarks are still primarily centered on general-domain preferences. In this work, we introduce LegalRewardBench, the first human-verified benchmark for evaluating reward models in the legal domain. The benchmark organizes legal preference evaluation into five capability levels: knowledge, understanding, analysis, decision, and writing, and preference examples are constructed through rubric-guided automatic judging combined with human verification. We evaluate three families of judges, covering both general and fine-tuned models, and generative and discriminative architectures. Experimental results show that strong general-purpose generative models are currently the most robust legal reward models, while existing fine-tuned reward models transfer less reliably to legal preference evaluation. We also conduct detailed comparisons of input organizations and training strategies.

title: Theory of Trotter Error with Variable-Weight Schedules
abstract: Trotterization is a widely used algorithm for simulating quantum evolutions and consists of approximating a target unitary through a local linear decomposition of its generator that is repeated over $N$ steps. We introduce {scheduled trotterization}, a variable-weight modification in which the coefficients of the local linear decomposition are allowed to change from step to step. Using the geometry of the Lie group of unitary operators, we express the global endpoint error as a product of transported local defects, whose leading terms are obtained by two applications of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, one inside each local step and one between different transported defects, separating the internal Trotter error from the external accumulation error. While we recover recent tighter bounds on the global approximation error when the weights are held fixed, the new framework allows us to propose a weight-varying schedule that significantly decreases the global error. For exact infinitesimal synthesis, we prove that this improves the usual fixed-weight $O(N^{-1})$ behavior to $O(N^{-2})$, without changing the basic pulse skeleton. We also extend the framework to imperfect infinitesimal synthesis, as arises in quantum gate synthesis problems, where admissible coefficients may only approximate the desired local corrections. In this case, the error is controlled by a local covering parameter measuring the quality of the available coefficient set. Numerical experiments for random $\SU(2)$ targets further support the predicted theoretical improvements. The results suggest a novel perspective for the analysis of Trotter errors, which can be treated as schedulable quantities to be coherently canceled at the endpoint.

title: Generalizable Representations for Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning
abstract: Multilingual models are essential in natural language processing (NLP), the field of enabling computational models to process and generate human language. These models are crucial for expanding information access across linguistic boundaries, with machine translation models being particularly central to this effort. However, with approximately 7,000 languages spoken worldwide, it is infeasible to acquire sufficient training data for every language. This data scarcity challenge highlights the importance of cross-lingual generalization, the ability to transfer knowledge learned from some languages to settings with little or no training data. Such generalization depends on a model's ability to learn internal representations that are shared and consistent across languages. While the \textit{classical} form of cross-lingual generalization involves training a model for a task in some languages and evaluating it on others, its application in machine translation is more complex as the input and output languages are inherently different. The directional nature of machine translation calls for \textit{compositional} generalization, which requires the model to combine knowledge from trained directions (e.g., English-to-German and German-to-French) to directly perform translation for unseen directions (e.g., English-to-French). Moreover, the pre-training fine-tuning paradigm introduces a crucial \textit{temporal} dimension to generalization. This perspective concerns how well a model's pre-trained capabilities are preserved after specializing on selected tasks or languages. This thesis addresses these three aspects of generalization: classical, compositional, and temporal. First, we investigate compositional generalization in translation models trained from scratch. We demonstrate that a primary reason why multilingual translation models fail to generalize compositionally is that their internal representations become highly entangled with information specific to the input language. We identify that this entanglement is reinforced by the residual connections within the model's architecture. By proposing a method that relaxes this structural constraint, we achieve substantial improvements on unseen translation directions. We then extend the investigation to the temporal dimension of generalization by incorporating pre-trained models. We observe that despite large-scale multilingual pre-training, a model's internal representations often remain highly specific to the input language. Moreover, when these models are specialized for particular translation directions, they are prone to catastrophic forgetting, which substantially degrades their existing capabilities. To counteract this, our work evaluates several established mitigation strategies from the literature and introduces a novel approach. Our proposed method produces a more interpretable view of the model's internal representations, although this benefit comes with a trade-off in translation quality. Our investigation then extends to large language models (LLMs), which operate as general-purpose instruction-following systems. For these models, which typically use a decoder-only architecture, we first identify the middle layers as the most effective positions for intervention. Building on this finding, we propose a modular and computationally efficient post-hoc method to enhance language invariance in the model's representations. This approach leads to substantial improvements in both classical cross-lingual transfer scenarios and the compositional generalization cases examined earlier. Lastly, we revisit classical cross-lingual transfer with a novel application for attribute-controlled machine translation. This method trains a classifier to distinguish text attributes in languages with available labeled data and then transfers this capability to guide translations for other languages lacking such resources. The approach operates on the model's internal activations rather than weights, making it suitable for scenarios where model weights must remain fully frozen. When compared to an oracle setup that updates the model weights, our activation-based method demonstrates stronger robustness against domain shifts. Each of the contributions above is situated within a model modification scope that aligns with evolving practices in the field, ranging from training models from scratch to performing post-hoc interventions on large pre-trained models. This thesis advances the development of multilingual NLP models that not only achieve strong performance under trained conditions but also acquire more generalizable and adaptable underlying representations.

title: Künstliche Intelligenz – Chance oder Risiko? Vortrag beim Katholischen Bildungswerk Frankenburg am Hausruck
abstract: lides of a general-audience evening talk (about 90 minutes plus discussion), given inGerman at the Catholic adult-education centre (Katholisches Bildungswerk) inFrankenburg am Hausruck, Upper Austria, on 13 October 2026. The talk explains, without formulas, what artificial intelligence can and cannot dotoday. Part 1 shows where AI already sits in everyday life (timetables, weather,navigation, licence-plate recognition, recommendations). Part 2 covers data as the rawmaterial, from monastic tithe registers to social media, the planned Google datacentre in Kronstorf, and open government data. Part 3 demonstrates AI agents on threelive examples: analysing the Frankenburg municipal council minutes 2021–2026, planninga bicycle tour, and a study of Alpine pumped-hydro storage. Part 4 contrastsopportunities (retinal-image diagnostics) with risks: hallucination, deepfakes,accountability, military use. It closes with three take-home messages. Includes the video shown in the talk: an AI-agent-generated flood visualisation(Perschling valley, September 2024) together with the slide explaining its limits.Text and the author's own figures are CC BY 4.0; third-party images and screenshotsare credited on the final slide and excluded from the licence.

title: Anti-Dual Vector Foil G: Composite Algebra and Composite Fiber Accounting of Weight-Dependent Annihilation Operators
abstract: Skeleton-layer annihilation operators are divided by the readout level of theirdecision rules into three types: skeleton-dependent, order-dependent, and absolutevalue-dependent. This paper studies two problems for weight-dependent annihilation operators: composite algebra and composite fiber accounting. On the composite algebra side, the composition table of threshold rules and ranking rules satisfies four operator identities: threshold composition takes the maximum parameter,ranking composition takes the sum of parameters, and both cross-type compositionpaths collapse, on every fixed network, to an initial segment of the global lexicographic order, whose parameter is a counting function of network weights andindices. The semigroup generated by threshold atoms and ranking atoms is closedunder composition; the class of elementary weight-dependent rules strictly containsthis generated semigroup, but in the sense of a uniformly predicate-syntacticallyclosed class it is the smallest rule class containing the two generators and closedunder composition and predicate conversion. The semigroup verdict exhibits coordinate differentiation: the skeleton-dependent end is trivially closed, the orderdependent end is closed under parameter addition, the pure-threshold end is closedunder taking extremes, and cross-coordinate composition forces an enlargement ofthe generated class. The readout level under composition is the supremum of thecomponents. On the fiber accounting side, in the standard discrete weight-latticemodel, the fiber cardinality of a threshold operator is determined jointly by thenumber of missing edges and the threshold, while the fiber cardinality of a ranking operator is given by a product formula involving tied indicator elements, andon subdomains of distinct weights it reduces to a falling factorial; all are verifiedby deterministic exhaustive enumeration over the whole space. Composite fibersare precisely described by a fiber decomposition identity: when composed with aweight-layer bijection, the composite fiber is equinumerous with the single-operatorfiber; when composed with a general weight-layer operator, the composite fiber isno smaller than the weight-layer end, and if the weight-layer map is surjective ontoits range, then the composite fiber is also no smaller than the annihilation end. Thedifference between the two composition orders is priced in bits; in the single-objectmodel, one spanning element corresponds to exactly one bit, and the redistributionof tied adjudication rights is its mechanism.

title: A UC-Secure Protocol for Privacy-Preserving Preferential Voting with Verifiable Encrypted Ballots
abstract: Preferential voting allows participants to rank multiple alternatives according to their preferences rather than being restricted to selecting a single option. Such mechanisms are used in national and local elections and, in decentralized governance, can be applied to committee selection, the prioritization of protocol upgrades or funding applications, and the choice of an electricity supplier or energy source. Of particular practical interest are systems in which participants have different stakes and their voting weights are proportional to those stakes. In the model considered in this work, each voter submits a complete ranking of the alternatives. The key technical challenge is to verify that an encrypted ballot encodes a valid ranking, that is, that exactly one rank is assigned to each alternative and each rank is used exactly once, without revealing the voter’s preferences. We propose a UC-secure protocol for privacy-preserving preferential voting with verifiable encrypted ballots. A ranking is represented as a permutation matrix whose entries are encrypted using an additively homomorphic cryptosystem. To verify ballot validity, each encrypted row of the matrix is accompanied by a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof that it is a unit vector. The encrypted rows are then homomorphically summed, and the resulting vector is checked against the all-ones vector. Together, these checks ensure that the encrypted matrix is a permutation matrix without revealing the ranking itself. Using an O(logm)-size unit-vector proof for each of the m rows yields O(mlogm) ballot-validity proof data, while the overall ballot size remains O(m2) because the encrypted matrix contains m2 ciphertexts. The protocol supports stake-weighted tallying and threshold decryption, so that only the final aggregate result is revealed. The UC security of the protocol is established in the random-oracle model under the Decisional Diffie–Hellman (DDH) assumption. The theoretical analysis shows that the computational complexity of generating and verifying a single ballot is O(m2) and that the ballot size is also O(m2), where m is the number of alternatives. The experimental results are consistent with this quadratic scaling: for 32 alternatives, the mean ballot-generation time is 87 ms, the mean verification time is 36 ms, and the reported cryptographic ballot payload is 106 KiB. These measurements indicate practical ballot-construction and verification costs for elections with a moderate number of alternatives.

The theoretical analysis shows that the computational complexity of generating and verifying a single ballot is O(m2) and that the ballot size is also O(m2), where m is the number of alternatives. The experimental results are consistent with this quadratic scaling: for 32 alternatives, the mean ballot-generation time is 87 ms, the mean verification time is 36 ms, and the reported cryptographic ballot payload is 106 KiB. These measurements indicate practical ballot-construction and verification costs for elections with a moderate number of alternatives.

title: TrackShield: An Efficient Runtime Defense Against Availability Attacks on High-Performance Real-Time Multi-Object Tracking
abstract: High-performance camera-based perception pipelines must sustain per-frame real-time budgets on resource-constrained embedded GPU platforms. Availability attacks such as SlowTrack inflate the persistent state of multi-object trackers: data-association workload accumulates across frames, so per-frame latency increases and drives the pipeline past its deadline. Detector- and NMS-layer defenses do not directly control this persistent tracker-side resource. We present TrackShield, a lightweight runtime resource-management layer that protects the tracker at the point where attack-induced workload accumulates. TrackShield combines low-overhead anomaly monitoring with staged birth capping, pruning of young or weakly matched tracks, and per-stage association-input admission control. Its hard admission guard provides a deterministic bound on admitted association workload, independently of the heuristic monitor. On a Jetson AGX Orin, TrackShield reduces attacked tracking-stage latency from $139.90$ to $6.27$\,ms and whole-pipeline P99 latency from $190.9$ to $48.8$\,ms, at a benign MOTA cost of $1.06$ points. As an availability defense, TrackShield focuses on keeping the tracker responsive under attack instead of recovering the full tracking accuracy degraded by adversarial detections.

title: Learning in Orbit: Onboard Training and Closed-Loop Attitude Control with a Thermal Segmentation Model on a Spacecraft
abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).

title: I2O2I-Nav: A Benchmark with a Modular Agent for Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor-to-Indoor Navigation
abstract: Service and delivery robots often need to complete long-horizon navigation missions spanning indoor and outdoor environments. Existing embodied navigation benchmarks primarily evaluate isolated stages or partial cross-domain journeys, providing limited support for assessing how heterogeneous navigation capabilities compose under continuous execution. We introduce I2O2I-Nav, a physics-enabled benchmark of 20 real-world composite scenes spanning over 115,000 square meters across multiple buildings and floors, with aligned 3DGS rendering and collision geometry. Its three-level evaluation progresses from independent primitives to two-stage compositions and complete four-stage I2O2I missions. Each stage starts from its predecessor's actual endpoint, while stage-conditional metrics track completion and localize failures along the mission. We further propose the MODULAR-Agent that coordinates frozen navigation policies through completion verification, stage handoffs, and bounded recovery. Evaluation across 1,374 episodes highlights the difficulty of continuous composition. The MODULAR-Agent achieves 40.5-76% success on individual primitives, but full I2O2I success remains low. Compared with a fixed policy chain using the same underlying policies, it more than doubles success on both Indoor-to-Outdoor (I2O) and Outdoor-to-Indoor (O2I), while improving full-mission success from 1.15% to 4.02%. Stage-wise analysis shows that the MODULAR-Agent enables more missions to reach the final object-navigation stage, where conditional success remains low, revealing challenges in both long-horizon stage execution and completion decisions.

title: DexStitch: Learning and Composing Dexterous Skills from Human Videos via Contact-Aware Robotic Inpainting
abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.

title: What Do Deepfake Audio Detectors Hear? From Self-Supervised Models to Audio LLMs
abstract: Real-world audio recordings for deepfake detection rarely consist solely of speech; they often are mixtures of speech and background events that themselves may also be synthetic. When processing these mixtures, it remains unclear whether detectors attend to the speech or the background event, and where their spectral evidence lies. We study this on the CompSpoof V2 database, whose mixtures pair independently real-or-fake speech and event components. Our results show that all systems detect fake events more accurately than fake speech. However, this performance gap is largely driven by poor generalization to an unseen fake speech domain, rather than a true difference in difficulty. Furthermore, sub-band probing reveals that the front-end encoder dictates where a countermeasure focuses its frequency evidence. To enable reliable deployment in real-world scenarios, future countermeasures should address out-of-domain generalization failures and carefully select front-end encoders aligned with their target acoustic evidence. Our source code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/nii-yamagishilab/AntiDeepfake-AudioLLM.

title: Tanawpamana: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Philippine Cultural Heritage Sites
abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models' recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.

title: Dimensional Collapse and Representation Entanglement: Context-Dependent Effects of Residual Connections in Over-Parameterized MLP Autoencoders
abstract: Residual connections have become a standard architectural component in deep learning, yet their effect on disentanglement in MLP autoencoders remains understudied. Recent work has shown that unsupervised disentanglement requires strong inductive biases, raising the question of whether common architectural choices can supply them. In this work, we investigate the failure modes of over-parameterized MLP autoencoders and test whether residual connections can mitigate them. We train small and large MLP autoencoders, with and without residual connections, on two datasets of varying complexity (dSprites and 3D Shapes), and evaluate them using MIG, DCI, and Effective Rank. Our experiments reveal two distinct failure modes: dimensional collapse on simple data, where the model converges to a shortcut solution using only a single latent dimension, and representation entanglement on complex data, where the model uses almost its full latent space but fails to separate the factors of variation. We find that residual connections partially mitigate dimensional collapse but are entirely ineffective against representation entanglement. These results suggest that architectural changes such as using residual connections alone are insufficient for disentanglement, and that an explicit disentanglement objective is likely required.

title: Operationalizing the QUETZAL Framework for Agent-Supported Instructional Design
abstract: This paper develops a conceptual architecture for the QUETZAL Agent, intended to support educators and instructional designers in transforming existing learning paths into adaptive learning offerings. Drawing on Paper2Agent and the Model Context Protocol, the design connects instructional decision logic, technical operationalization, and agentic interaction. An inspectable adaptation specification makes proposals, rationales, and responsibilities traceable. Human decision authority and iterative review are central design principles. A hypothetical use case illustrates the architecture; its practical effectiveness remains to be investigated empirically.

title: Going Faster: Privacy-Preserving Shortest Paths from Start to End
abstract: Finding shortest paths in graphs is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem with numerous applications, e. g., in graph centrality measures, computational biology, and business process analysis. To address privacy constraints in such applications, Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) protocols can compute the lengths of shortest paths on secret-shared graphs. Many such protocols have been proposed in the past, but they only compute the lengths of the shortest paths and not the paths themselves.

title: The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge
abstract: International challenges have become the standard for developing and benchmarking biomedical image analysis methods using centralized multi-institutional data. Federated learning (FL) describes a paradigm-shift on multi-institutional collaborations, where models are trained across institutions while their data are always retained locally. The Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge, first held in 2021, was the first challenge dedicated to FL in medical imaging and editions in 2022 and 2024 pushed the frontiers of real-world method validation. FeTS++ 2027 returns after a two-year gap with a substantially larger and more diverse cohort, and with the two "pluses" that name the challenge: an official classification task alongside segmentation, and a move of the infrastructure to NVIDIA FLARE (NVFlare). Built on the clinically acquired, multi-institutional multi-parametric MRI data of the BraTS 2025 Lighthouse challenge, FeTS++ spans gliomas and meningiomas across patient cohorts from institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and focuses on ranking submitted methodological approaches according to their model utility and an efficiency-aware score. Task 1 asks participants to find the best strategy for aggregating knowledge from per-institution segmentation models, while Task 2 asks them to distinguish glioma from meningioma under the same federated protocol, in which the entity label is heavily confounded with the site of origin.

title: Beyond the Encoder: Object-Centric Representations Emerging from Segmentation Foundation Models
abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for downstream tasks with limited data, typically through representations obtained from their encoders. However, foundation models trained for structured tasks such as segmentation also form object-specific representations during task execution, whose transferability remains largely unexplored. We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.

We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.

title: COMPASS: Contextual Moment Prior Alignment for Generalizable AIGI Detection
abstract: Generalizable AI-generated image (AIGI) and deepfake detection remain challenging due to the asymmetry phenomenon, where adaptation to limited training distributions can degrade the transferable representations of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs). Recent subspace adaptation methods mitigate this issue by freezing high-magnitude principal components while adapting the residual subspace. However, such magnitude-based decomposition is data-agnostic and does not explicitly account for target-relevant semantics, potentially leading to semantic misalignment. We propose COMPASS (COntextual Moment Prior Alignment for Subspace Separation), a data-aware subspace adaptation framework that uses a small unlabeled Semantic Proxy Set to estimate target activation statistics. COMPASS incorporates activation covariance into the decomposition of pre-trained weights, preserving target-relevant representations as a stable semantic reference while the residual adapter learns forgery-related variations. The proxy calibration requires no gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong generalization across cross-dataset, cross-method, joint cross-dataset-method, and open-world cross-generator evaluations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both Deepfake and AIGI detection benchmarks.

title: Chromatic Block-Gibbs p-Bit Decoding of QLDPC Codes
abstract: We introduce a parallel decoder for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes based on probabilistic bits (p-bits), tunable stochastic binary units controlled by local fields. The idea is that predicted error configurations, interpreted as explanations of the observed syndrome, are updated stochastically using local Gibbs conditionals, while a progressively strengthened parity penalty drives the search toward syndrome-valid configurations. A coloring of the decoding graph enables parallel block updates, and independent replicas and restarts provide trajectory diversity. The best candidate encountered during the search is returned, mirroring the candidate-selection strategy of recent ensemble decoders. At the stated update budgets, the resulting logical error rates are on par with leading decoders under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise. While the total number of variable resamplings can be substantially larger than the message-update count of BP-based alternatives, the numerical results establish constraint-annealed p-bit dynamics as a competitive stochastic alternative for QLDPC decoding and motivate further study of hardware-native implementations.

title: DPP-1: Data-Plane Poisoning via Metadata — Poison In, Nothing Out (67/67 Poisoned Instances Decision-Identical, 7/7 Canaries Absent from Outputs)
abstract: DPP-1 — Data-Plane Poisoning via Metadata: the third leg of the Oct 13 adversarial triad. SBR-2 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23345734) attacked mid-learning; H-INV-2 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23345859) attacked the ledger. This battery attacks the inputs themselves: adversarial content planted directly in the fields the mesh ingests. A deterministically derived poisoned corpus (underlying metrics unchanged; poison only in metadata) planted instruction injections, forged confidence overrides, credential/PHI/wallet lookalikes, forged severity, fake playbook links, and pattern-forcing payloads — each with a unique synthetic canary marker — on every 3rd instance. All 5 falsifiers PASS (first run): every poisoned instance produced a decision tuple byte-identical to the clean baseline (zero decision effect); all 7 canaries absent from every persisted output artifact (redaction-at-ingestion held); the poisoned run's 40-epoch weight trajectory and 2,646-crossing journal byte-identical to the clean baseline (learning uncontaminated); 106/106 lineage controls valid; artifact hygiene clean. Note: the poisoned corpus file is the attack instrument and intentionally contains the planted synthetic canaries (all explicitly fake); the falsifier is their absence from all outputs. No real credentials or personal data anywhere. Scope honesty: proves THIS registered instrument under THIS frozen battery — not a universal claim about every data pipeline or untested poison classes. Operator authorization recorded as GO + timestamp per the operator-privacy doctrine. Dual Mesh Benchmark: MEASURED for the DeepSeek column (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23345241); all other figures NOT MEASURED. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects.

title: Optical and Photonic Computing for Deep Learning Acceleration: Silicon Photonics, Mach-Zehnder Meshes, and Wavelength-Division Multiplexing
abstract: Abstract—The relentless exponential scaling of foundation models and transformer architectures has pushed conventional silicon complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) digital accelerators (GPUs, TPUs) toward fundamental thermodynamic and interconnect boundaries. Joule heating, resistance-capacitance (RC) interconnect delay scaling, and the 'memory wall' severely constrain energy efficiency and compute density. Optical Computing and Integrated Silicon Photonics (SiPh) establish an analog non-Von Neumann hardware paradigm that executes fundamental linear algebra operations—specifically General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication (GEMM)—at the speed of light with near-zero runtime energy dissipation. By encoding vector-matrix activations into coherent optical wave fields and modulating light through cascaded Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI) meshes, Micro-Ring Resonator (MRR) banks, and Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM) waveguides, photonic tensor processing units (PTPUs) execute analog matrix multiplications in continuous time with sub-nanosecond propagation latencies. However, translating integrated photonic circuits into production deep learning accelerators introduces profound optoelectronic engineering bottlenecks: analog noise accumulation across deep optical meshes, severe thermal phase drift, limited electro-optic Digital-to-Analog / Analog-to-Digital (DAC/ADC) conversion resolution, non-linear activation implementation hurdles, and wafer-scale optical footprint scaling. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of integrated photonic computing for deep neural network acceleration. We formalize the Clements and Reck unitary matrix decomposition algorithms over reconfigurable MZI topologies, derive the optical transmission transfer matrix under optical carrier phase error perturbations, and establish energy-per-MAC physical thermodynamic bounds across electro-optic conversion interfaces. Furthermore, we construct an empirical co-simulation and hardware testbed benchmarking silicon photonic meshes against state-of-the-art CMOS accelerators (NVIDIA H100, Google TPU v5p) across vision transformers, large language model attention heads, and resonant graph convolutions. Our empirical findings demonstrate that a 64x64 integrated MZI photonic mesh achieves a 58.4x improvement in energy-delay product (EDP) over 4nm digital CMOS cores, sustaining up to 128 Tera-Operations per Second per Watt (TOPS/W) at 4-bit to 8-bit equivalent precision, while active thermo-optic phase stabilization preserves 98.2% baseline classification accuracy. Finally, we establish open research directions in all-optical non-linear activation functions, co-packaged optical memory architectures, and wafer-scale photonic interconnect scaling. Index Terms—Photonic Computing, Silicon Photonics (SiPh), Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI), Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM), Optical Neural Networks (ONNs), Matrix-Vector Multiplication, Energy-Efficient Accelerators.

title: Orbital Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Relativistic Entanglement Distribution via LEO Satellite Constellations: Compensating Spacetime Curvature, Dynamic Doppler Shifts, and Atmospheric Turbulence in Intercontinental Space-to-Ground Entanglement Routing
abstract: Abstract: Terrestrial fiber-optic quantum networks are subject to exponential photon attenuation (≈ 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm), constraining unrepeatered ground quantum key distribution (QKD) and entanglement distribution to distances below a few hundred kilometers. While quantum repeaters remain technologically nascent, intercontinental sovereign security mandates unhackable, physical-layer cryptographic connectivity across transoceanic baselines. Satellite-based quantum communications operating in Low Earth Orbit (LEO, altitude h ≈ 500–800 km) provide a transformative solution by exploiting near-vacuum propagation for the vast majority of the optical path, bypassing terrestrial exponential loss. However, high-velocity LEO satellite platforms (v ≈ 7.6 km/s) introduce severe relativistic and atmospheric distortions that rapidly destroy quantum coherence: (1) kinematic Doppler shifts (Δν/ν ≈ ± 2.5 × 10^-5) and general relativistic gravitational redshifts alter photon wavepackets and relative phase trajectories; (2) dynamic spacetime curvature induces Wigner phase rotations on polarization-entangled states; and (3) atmospheric turbulence creates beam wandering, wavefront aberration, and photon arrival time jitter across the troposphere (0–15 km). This monograph establishes the theoretical framework, mathematical formulation, and solid-state engineering architecture for the PHOENIX_ORBIT space-to-ground quantum communications network. We derive: (1) an exact relativistic transformation matrix incorporating Kerr-Schwarzschild spacetime metric perturbations and orbital kinematics, coupled to an ultra-fast electro-optic dynamic phase compensator operating with sub-picosecond latency; (2) an adaptive optics (AO) closed-loop architecture combining high-bandwidth tip-tilt mirrors and deformable piezo-actuators calibrated to the local Fried parameter r_0 and Greenwood frequency f_G; (3) an entanglement routing protocol linking space-borne spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) sources to ground-based PHOENIX_ROUTER quantum data centers; and (4) an asymptotic security proof verifying Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) Bell inequality violation (S ≥ 2√2 − ε) under non-inertial reference frame drift. Our architecture achieves a continuous secret key rate exceeding 1.2 Mbps per satellite pass with a quantum bit error rate QBER < 1.4%, providing an unassailable physical-layer foundation for global sovereign data sovereignty.

title: Model Context Protocol for Agentic Systems
abstract: This chapter provides a comprehensive examination of the model context protocol (MCP), a context-oriented, general-purpose protocol for tool integration in agentic systems. MCP represents the most promising approach for context-oriented tool integration in connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) applications, providing standardized interfaces for primitive discovery and invocation. The chapter covers MCP architecture, implementation, and application in CAV systems. It examines how MCP operationalizes distributed cognition, enabling bidirectional context flow between AI models and external systems. The chapter addresses the fundamental context problem CAV systems face and demonstrates how MCP enables agents to interact with external tools and services while maintaining context coherence and system integration.

title: DoReMe: Dual optimization of Reconstruction and Motion estimation for self-navigated free-breathing abdominal MRI using Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Purpose: Free-breathing abdominal MRI is limited by respiratory motion, which introduces image artifacts and k-space inconsistencies. Existing reconstruction approaches often depend on pre-estimated motion fields or external respiratory surrogate signals. We propose a coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm for self-navigated free-breathing acquisition, in which motion is represented by compact Gaussian primitives and jointly refined with the image estimates during iterative reconstruction. Methods: An iterative reconstruction that alternates between data consistency updates and motion modelling was proposed. Respiratory motion was represented using Gaussian primitives. A Gaussian splatting was integrated into the reconstruction algorithm. The method was evaluated on self-navigated free-breathing Cartesian gradient-echo (GRE) acquisition in four healthy volunteers, including retrospective scan shortening experiments, and was compared with regularized compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction. Results: Respiratory motion states were reconstructed in approximately 1.5 min. Compared with CS, the proposed method improved visual image quality, particularly in coronal liver views, and better preserved anatomical structures in retrospectively shortened acquisitions. These findings provide proof of concept for the proposed method. Conclusion: The proposed coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm improved visual image quality compared with CS alone. Gaussian primitives provided a compact and sufficiently flexible representation of nonrigid respiratory motion with practical runtime, supporting further scanner integration and validation in larger cohorts.

title: MIST: Multi-Scale Spatial Context for Gene Expression Prediction from Histology
abstract: Predicting spatial gene expression from standard H&E images could extend molecular analysis to tissues without spatial transcriptomic measurements. A standard Transformer applies self-attention over spots but ignores where each spot sits in the tissue, whereas a spot's molecular state depends on tissue context at multiple spatial scales. Building on this insight, we introduce MIST, a Multi-context Spatial Transformer that augments the self-attention backbone with two context pathways applied in every layer: a coordinate-invariant local pathway that attends over spatial k-nearest-neighbor spots, and a slide pathway that broadcasts a whole-slide summary to every spot; the model predicts all spots in a single forward pass. Because coordinates enter only through pairwise distances, the local pathway is invariant to translations, rotations, and reflections when image features are fixed. In intra-cohort evaluation across six human organ cohorts from HEST-1k, MIST improves mean Pearson correlation over the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.7%, 11.6%, and 11.4% for 10-, 50-, and 100-gene panels, respectively, with the lowest average MSE and MAE. MIST further improves leave-one-organ-out transfer by 6.0% over the next strongest baseline, attains the best expression-derived domain recovery (highest mean ARI and NMI at every clustering resolution, and higher NMI than the closest baseline on 84% of held-out slides), and reproduces spatial expression patterns of selected cancer-marker genes. Together, these results show that adding local and slide context to a vanilla Transformer backbone is an effective approach to spatial gene expression prediction from histology.

title: SkipWorld: Latent Skip Planning with Distilled World Models for Efficient Visual Navigation
abstract: World-model-based visual navigation enables action planning by predicting future states under candidate trajectories. However, long-horizon rollout remains challenging: models are often trained with ground-truth visual histories but deployed in closed-loop prediction, and evaluating many candidates with step-by-step rollout is computationally expensive. We propose SkipWorld, a latent skip planning framework for efficient visual navigation. SkipWorld introduces three components: (i) Latent AutoRoll, which trains a world model to recursively roll out future states in latent space, reducing the mismatch between training and closed-loop inference; (ii) SkipDistill, which distills the latent autoregressive model into a skip world model that directly predicts long-stride future latent states; and (iii) Skip-then-Refine Planning, a dual-model coarse-to-fine planner that first filters candidate trajectories with the skip model and then reranks selected candidates with the stronger autoregressive model. title: FlowSim: Rendering-Free Closed-Loop Simulation for Evaluating End-to-End Driving Systems
abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end (E2E) driving systems typically relies on generating sensor observations and re-processing them through the perception encoder, introducing substantial computational cost and a sim2real gap between simulated and real sensor observations. In this paper, we ask a more fundamental question: is image-space simulation necessary for closed-loop evaluation of E2E driving systems? We propose FlowSim, a rendering-free simulation paradigm that predicts the internal latent representation directly from a previous latent and target-frame symbolic scene conditions. The predicted latent is then processed by the original frozen downstream modules, eliminating image rendering and perception re-encoding. Explicit cross-frame agent association improves latent transition prediction and rollout stability, while variable-horizon simulation enables long-horizon prediction from a common real anchor without accumulating intermediate rollout errors. Experiments on nuScenes and NavSim demonstrate that FlowSim preserves downstream behavior competitively with, and often exceeds image-space simulation in source-to-reference agreement across variable simulation horizons and both dense and sparse latent representations. By predicting the latent directly, both instantiations of FlowSim simulate each step in 0.04--0.06s, substantially faster than the image-space simulation methods they are compared against. These results establish FlowSim as an efficient and practical alternative to conventional image-space simulation methods.

title: Agentic4PDM: Host-Governed Evidence Admissibility for Industrial Fault Diagnosis
abstract: We study industrial fault diagnosis as a classification task that assigns sensor time-series windows to predefined health states or fault types. Scarce labels and changing operating conditions make repeated training of specialized classifiers costly. Yet structures such as periodicity, trends, and transients can remain diagnostically informative and be examined through reusable analytical tools. LLM agents can select and interpret these tools, but fixed rules or training-derived guidance may not resolve each signal's ambiguity, while unconstrained interpretation may overstate weak or conflicting results. We introduce Agentic4PDM, a framework that separates adaptive investigation from control over evidence use. LLM agents compare each signal with labeled references from every candidate class, identify unresolved distinctions, and propose follow-up measurements. A deterministic software controller, called the host, enforces contract-checked gated adjudication (CCGA): it checks requests, requires commitment to a complete tool batch before results are observed, and assigns evidence roles based on tool checks against labeled references. These roles distinguish corroborative support from advisory information. The Judge Agent proposes a diagnosis, while the controller checks protocol compliance and records the investigation. Agentic4PDM supports training-free diagnosis using pretrained representations and labeled references without task-specific diagnostic models, and a standard setting that additionally investigates trained-model predictions. Experiments on selected bearing and motor diagnosis challenges and an unfiltered industrial test set supplied by our customer show gains in aggregate macro F1 over the evaluated diagnostic and agentic baselines. Ablations further support the value of the governed workflow.

title: Physical-Field-Bridged Material Parameter Inference from Multi-View Deformation Videos
abstract: Estimating simulation-ready material parameters from visual observations is crucial for deformable-object manipulation but challenging because material properties are only indirectly revealed through physical responses. We introduce physical-field-bridged material inference, a single-pass framework that uses dense physical responses to connect multi-view RGB deformation videos with constitutive-type classification and continuous parameter regression. Unlike inverse-physics methods requiring per-scene reconstruction, online tuning, or simulation-in-the-loop optimization, our model predicts force/contact masks, projected motion-flow fields, and projected stress-response maps, then conditions material inference on these fields to reduce reliance on appearance or category shortcuts. We construct DeformFieldBench, a 3DGS MPM learning environment comprising 5,000 simulations across 100 object shapes and five mechanically informative loading modes, with dense pixel-aligned physical supervision. Our method achieves the best median errors on all four continuous parameters, improves stress-hotspot recall from 0.0762 to 0.5121, and attains 0.8676 SSIM/36.82 dB PSNR in same-simulator replay on unseen objects. Under a protocol-matched GSO evaluation, inference and future-state prediction take approximately 30 seconds, compared with 15-120 minutes for per-scene optimization. The method also yields measurable replay agreement on five real-world sequences. These results support dense physical fields as an effective bridge for fast material inference, while cross-simulator and real-world tests reveal remaining domain and identifiability gaps.

title: Sociotechnical Aspects of Tor Relay Rejection
abstract: In 2019, the Tor Project enforced an end-of-life (EoL) policy for Tor versions, leading to the rejection of outdated relays, amounting to a notable fraction of consensus weight. While this policy aids network maintenance, reduces backporting efforts, and shortens vulnerability exposure, its sociotechnical implications remain unstudied.

title: SBR-2: Hot-State Adversarial Exam — Governance Invariants Hold During Active Learning (Trajectory Identity, 20/20 Probes Rejected)
abstract: SBR-2 — Hot-State Adversarial Exam: the first adversarial examination of the bounded-learning hemispheric mesh in its HOT state (mid-epoch, weights in flight). A preregistered, non-adaptive 5-probe battery (forged authority, under-confidence heal with adversarial confidence payload, orphan lineage injections attacking the journaled-crossing invariant, runtime playbook mutation, forged roster row) fired at epochs 5/15/25/35 of the T2C-converged 40-epoch bounded training regime. All 5 falsifiers PASS. Governance roster SHA byte-identical through every adversarial epoch (H-INV-1); 20/20 probes journaled with zero mesh deltas attributable to any probe (H-INV-2); zero side effects; and trajectory identity — the adversarial run's weight-vector trajectory is byte-identical epoch-for-epoch to a clean control run. Adversarial load could not nudge a single weight mid-learning. Scope honesty: proves THIS registered instrument (frozen corpus, 32-node mesh, frozen 3-playbook roster, bounded learning rule) under THIS frozen probe battery only — not a universal production claim. No adaptive probing, no re-runs. The preregistration records operator authorization as GO + timestamp per the operator-privacy doctrine effective 2026-10-13; a redaction note is disclosed in-place. Complements SBR-1 (at-rest exam, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23331224), AUTH-1 (channel authority, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23332203), XPLAT-5 (engine parity, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23332291): the invariance evidence now includes adversary-present-during-learning. Dual Mesh Benchmark: MEASURED for the DeepSeek column (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23345241); all other figures NOT MEASURED. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects.

title: Search-Trajectory Patterns as Feedback for Adaptive Metaheuristic Configuration Control
abstract: Adaptive decisions are often based on algorithm-specific feedback or simple indicators that provide limited information about the evolving search dynamics. This work investigates explicit pattern-based analysis of the search trajectory as a source of feedback for adaptive configuration control. A trajectory-driven framework is proposed in which Derivative Dynamic Time Warping (DDTW) analyzes the recent best-so-far fitness trajectory against reference patterns representing sustained progress and lack of progress. The resulting information regulates switching between predefined exploration- and exploitation-oriented parameter configurations. Two control strategies are introduced: Binary-Simple, which reacts directly to trajectory evidence associated with a plateau, and Binary-Complex, which incorporates multiple search conditions, temporal persistence, and asymmetric switching. The framework is evaluated on 27 Multidimensional Knapsack Problem instances using BPSO, GA, BGWO, and BDE, with 31 independent runs per condition. Results show that no fixed configuration consistently dominates across metaheuristics and instances, while the effects of trajectory-driven adaptation depend on the underlying algorithm. Across 108 metaheuristic–instance conditions, Binary-Complex achieves the best mean rank (2.13). The Friedman test detects an overall difference among strategies (p=7.73×10−5); Bonferroni-Dunn post-hoc comparisons favor Binary-Complex over both fixed configurations, but do not establish a difference from Binary-Simple. Moreover, a common trajectory-analysis parameterization produces different switching behaviors across the evaluated metaheuristics. These findings support explicit search-trajectory pattern analysis as a viable feedback mechanism for adaptive configuration control across different population-based metaheuristics.

title: An explainable AI framework using wearable IMU-based motion sensing for estimating and explaining motor skill improvement in school-based Baduanjin education
abstract: Estimation of individual skill improvement within specific school-based physical education units remains methodologically underdeveloped, with existing approaches typically lacking external validation and interpretability. Because the full model incorporates training-load features aggregated across the same temporal window as the outcome, it is epistemologically retrospective; readers should not interpret it as a prospectively deployable prediction tool. This study aimed at developing and externally validating an explainable machine learning ensemble to retrospectively explain and estimate standardized skill gain (Δz) in Baduanjin (eight-section brocade) qigong, a mandatory traditional martial arts skill in the Chinese national PE curriculum, among students from four schools ( n = 727). A stacking meta-learner composed of five candidate algorithms, including XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, LASSO, and MLP, was trained using biomechanical, psycho-cognitive, and semester-aggregated training-load features obtained from the development cohort (Schools A + B, n = 486) and then validated against two geographically independent but regionally situated cohorts (Schools C + D, n = 241). Because the training-load features were aggregated across the full 16-week semester, the model functions as a retrospective semester-level estimation framework rather than a prospective early-warning tool. The model yielded an external validation R² of 0.691 (95% CI: 0.661–0.718), with robust subgroup performance across gender, initial skill quartiles, and sport types. SHAP-based interpretability analysis identified exercise self-efficacy as the highest-ranking modifiable feature in model-derived importance, with its predictive contribution predominantly associated with the training-response component rather than baseline level. A baseline-only sensitivity model excluding semester-aggregated training-load variables retained moderate external validity (R² = 0.573), indicating that prospective application at semester onset is feasible in principle but at substantially reduced precision. These findings suggest that, within this dataset and model specification, psycho-cognitive features contributed more strongly to model estimations than biomechanical features.

title: Mitigating Domain Shift and Dataset Bias in Deep Learning Models for Cancer Diagnostics
abstract: The translation of deep learning architectures from controlled experimental settings into real-world cancer diagnostics is heavily bottlenecked by domain shift and demographic bias. While models routinely achieve near-perfect retrospective performance on internal datasets, validation across external multicenter cohorts incurs a systemic and severe performance degradation, with an average metric drop of 0.16 AUC. This review provides a comprehensive metasynthesis of contemporary algorithmic mitigation paradigms designed to alleviate distribution discrepancies, evaluating techniques ranging from classical stain normalization and adversarial feature alignment to test-time adaptation and large-scale self-supervised pathology foundation models. Our analysis reveals a critical dichotomy between raw diagnostic performance and algorithmic equity: current optimization frameworks that successfully elevate aggregate macro metrics frequently do so by obscuring or actively exacerbating underlying demographic and subpopulation disparities. To achieve safe, equitable, and universally reliable clinical artificial intelligence, the field must transcend static validation habits. We outline a future roadmap anchored on three critical axes: establishing intersectional disparity indices as primary regulatory endpoints, standardizing multivendor metadata-rich benchmarks, and prioritizing.

title: The cost of classically simulating quantum communication is as high as it could be
abstract: A long-standing open question is to characterize the classical communication cost of simulating the correlations arising from measurements on finite-dimensional quantum systems. We consider this question in the prepare-and-measure scenario. First we construct a classical simulation model involving a finite average number of bits of one-way communication that simulates exactly the correlations arising from arbitrary $d$-dimensional quantum states and arbitrary measurements. Second, we show that no classical simulation protocol involving a finite average message dimension can exist for $d\geq 4$, hence strengthening a recent result of de Gois, Santos and Vieira. Our first result relies on a more general simulation theorem which can be applied to certain continuous variable (i.e. infinite-dimensional) quantum systems, and even beyond quantum theory, e.g. to generalized probabilistic theories. In particular, we show that multimode Gaussian states of bounded average energy and general Gaussian measurements admit an exact classical simulation with a finite expected number of bits. Overall, our results show that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially as high as it could be.

title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
abstract: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.

title: Building ACLA-PH: A Multiplatform Corpus of Philippine Gayspeak
abstract: The rapid expansion of digitally mediated communication has transformed the nature of linguistic data and challenged traditional approaches to corpus construction. These challenges are particularly evident in documenting Philippine Gayspeak, a dynamic and multilingual linguistic repertoire characterized by continual lexical innovation, multimodal communication, and platform-dependent interaction. This study introduces ACLA-PH (A Corpus Linguistic Approach to Philippine Gayspeak), a multiplatform corpus designed to document contemporary Philippine Gayspeak across publicly accessible digital environments. The findings demonstrate that constructing corpora for rapidly evolving digital discourse requires methodological principles that extend beyond traditional corpus linguistic practices. title: MedFusion: When Does a Chest X-Ray Improve ICU Risk Prediction?
abstract: This study asks when a chest X-ray (CXR) adds prognostic value to an ICU risk model, and whether the gain comes from the ordering pattern (counts and timing of X-ray studies) or from image content (CheXpert labels extracted from radiology reports). We linked three PhysioNet datasets: MIMIC-IV v3.1 (hospital and ICU records), MIMIC-CXR-JPG v2.0.0 (chest X-ray metadata and CheXpert labels), and MIMIC-IV-ED (emergency department triage vitals). The analysis cohort comprises 16,447 ED-admitted ICU stays from 13,001 patients (2011-2016). We compare gradient-boosting models with and without CXR ordering features and CheXpert content labels, across four prediction times (t0 = 0, 6, 12, 24 hours after ICU admission), for two outcomes: hospital death and new invasive ventilation within 24 hours of t0. At t0 = 0h we additionally include ED triage vitals in the EHR baseline and apply a 1-hour grace period to exclude stays where ventilation preceded the prediction window. Pre-specified success criterion: ΔAUROC ≥ 0.01 with the 95% bootstrap confidence interval entirely above zero. Primary finding: CXR ordering adds +0.017 AUROC and CheXpert content adds +0.005 AUROC for ventilation prediction at t0 = 0h, both exceeding the threshold, both surviving the addition of ED triage vitals. By t0 = 6h, both gains return to zero. For hospital death at any prediction time, neither ordering nor content adds meaningfully (all ΔAUROC < 0.003). Conclusion: A chest X-ray adds clinically meaningful prognostic information only at ICU admission and only for a chest-specific outcome. The gain is independent of ED triage severity and vanishes within 6 hours.

title: LayerCanvas: Infographic Generation in AI Learning Assistants via Hybrid Layer-Set Diffusion
abstract: Online learning platforms are increasingly deploying AI assistants to provide personalized, on-demand tutoring. These can leverage infographics to communicate complex information and improve the learning experience. However, automating effective infographic generation remains a challenging task, requiring a combination of visual richness with precise typography, structured layouts, and continued editability. Existing representation methods satisfy these goals only in part: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) representations preserve geometry, hierarchy, and text but provide limited aesthetic flexibility, while raster diffusion models produce richer appearances by flattening content and layout into a single image. Conditioning a diffusion model on a rasterized SVG does not resolve this conflict because the raster preserves approximate placement but discards element ownership, occlusion relationships, and the structure needed to modify and recompose the result. We introduce LayerCanvas, a hybrid approach that retains SVG as the semantic, structural, and typographic program while using diffusion to aestheticize non-text content. Rather than generating one flattened raster, LayerCanvas partitions SVG elements into z-ordered sets of mutually non-overlapping elements and processes them through communicating parallel RGB generation streams. The resulting layers are independently editable and deterministically recomposed, while text is rendered from preserved vector metadata. Our approach combines rich visual synthesis with accurate typography and localized editing. LayerCanvas substantially improves text fidelity over state-of-the-art raster image generators while achieving the highest overall aesthetic quality. We further demonstrate non-destructive content editing, localization, asset reuse, and animation.

title: Meta-Video: Efficient Standardized Evaluation for Video Understanding
abstract: Video understanding benchmarks are the primary yardstick for measuring progress in video-language modeling, and a growing body of work relies on them to claim improvements. The reported benchmark scores in these works, however, are almost always produced by frameworks (e.g., lmms eval) used as black boxes: certain evaluation choices like frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting are inherited from preset defaults and seldom inspected carefully. We show these unexamined choices are a major source of variance. Even for the same model checkpoint, evaluation configuration alone can shift accuracy by up to 19.5pp. Hence, it is unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in capability or differences in evaluation setup. Moreover, many benchmark samples offer little evidence of visual capability, since they can be answered without the video, and the full suites are expensive to evaluate. We address these issues in two parts. First, we curate existing suites for discriminability and efficiency, producing Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark over 791 videos spanning diverse tasks and durations, which largely preserves model rankings, at 5 times inference speedup for a full-frame count sweep experiment (4-128 frames). Second, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol by sweeping the configuration space to isolate choices that measurably affect results, distill them into best practices and reporting standards, and release reproducible reference scores across five models and seven benchmarks. We hope that the proposed evaluation framework and the Meta-Video benchmark will support video understanding research by providing a reproducible and efficient foundation to measure progress in a reliable way.
